q: India's Union Budget is presented by the:
opts: Finance Minister of India in Parliament
explain: Union Budget: presented by Finance Minister in Parliament (Lok Sabha) on February 1 (changed from last day of February in 2017, by Finance Minister Arun Jaitley). Consists of Revenue Budget (tax/non-tax income + current expenditure) and Capital Budget (assets/liabilities). First Budget: James Wilson (1860) under British. P. Chidambaram presented most Budgets (9 times).

q: SARFAESI Act 2002 enables:
opts: Banks to recover NPAs by seizing secured assets without going to court
explain: SARFAESI (Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002): banks can: (1) issue demand notice to defaulter, (2) take symbolic/physical possession of collateral after 60 days without court intervention, (3) sell/manage asset or assign to ARC (Asset Reconstruction Company). Major tool for NPA recovery along with DRT (Debt Recovery Tribunal).

q: The Chennai-Bengaluru Industrial Corridor (CBIC) is aimed at:
opts: Developing manufacturing clusters along the Chennai-Bengaluru highway
explain: Chennai-Bengaluru Industrial Corridor (CBIC): planned industrial corridor along NH-48 through Tamil Nadu (Hosur, Krishnagiri, Ranipet) and Karnataka. Focus: electronics manufacturing, automobiles, IT hardware, textiles. Part of India's industrial corridor development program along with DMIC (Delhi-Mumbai), AKIC (Amritsar-Kolkata).

q: The term 'crop diversification' in agriculture means:
opts: Shifting from monoculture to multiple crops
explain: Crop Diversification: growing a variety of crops (different from traditional cereal monoculture). Benefits: reduces market and weather risk, improves soil health, nutrition security, higher value crops (horticulture → higher income than cereals). Government promotes with MSP for pulses and oilseeds, cluster development programs, and horticulture development programs.

q: India's largest public sector undertaking (PSU) by revenue is:
explain: Indian Oil Corporation (IOC): India's largest company by revenue (~Rs 8 lakh crore). It is a Fortune 500 company (ranked ~94th globally). Refines and markets petroleum products through its extensive pipeline and retail network (~30,000 outlets). Other large PSUs: ONGC (oil exploration), BPCL, HPCL, Coal India, SBI, LIC, NTPC.

q: The 'velocity of money' in economics refers to:
opts: Rate at which money circulates in the economy
explain: Velocity of Money (V): average number of times a unit of currency is spent in a period. Fisher's Equation of Exchange: MV = PQ (M = money supply, V = velocity, P = price level, Q = real output). If velocity falls (people hoard money), money supply must increase to maintain same GDP. Velocity fell sharply during COVID-19 (people hoarded).

q: GDP stands for:
explain: GDP = total monetary value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a given period. GDP = C + I + G + (X−M).

q: The Keynesian theory of employment argues:
opts: Aggregate demand determines output and employment
Markets always self-correct to full employment (classical view)
Supply creates its own demand (Say's Law)
explain: John Maynard Keynes ('General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money,' 1936): challenged classical economics. Key ideas: markets don't always self-correct (can settle at equilibrium below full employment), aggregate demand determines output, government spending can fill the 'demand gap' during recessions (fiscal stimulus). Explains Great Depression and counter-cyclical policy.

q: The phenomenon of 'Dutch Disease' refers to:
opts: A resource boom that appreciates the currency and hurts other exports
explain: Dutch Disease: named after Netherlands' North Sea gas discovery (1959). Large foreign currency inflows from resource boom → currency appreciates → manufacturing becomes uncompetitive → deindustrialization. Examples: Nigeria (oil), Venezuela (oil). Prevention: sovereign wealth funds (Norway), diversification strategies.

q: Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC) is chaired by:
explain: FSDC (2010): apex body for financial stability, inter-regulatory coordination, and financial sector development. Chaired by Finance Minister. Members: heads of RBI, SEBI, IRDA, PFRDA, IBBI, FMC, DEA.

q: The 'brain drain' problem in developing economies like India refers to:
opts: Emigration of highly skilled professionals abroad
Internal migration from villages to cities (rural-urban migration)
explain: Brain Drain: emigration of talented, educated citizens to USA, UK, Canada, Australia etc. India loses significant numbers of IIT/IIM graduates, doctors, and scientists. Counter-argument: remittances ($100B), diaspora investment, knowledge transfer. Brain Drain vs Brain Gain vs Brain Circulation. Recently: 'reverse brain drain' as some Indian-origin professionals return.

q: The headquarters of the World Bank is in:
explain: The World Bank Group is headquartered in Washington D.C., USA. It provides loans and grants to poorer countries for development projects. IMF is also headquartered in Washington D.C.

q: India's Consumer Price Index (CPI) gives the highest weight to which category?
explain: CPI (Combined, Base 2012): Food and beverages have the highest weight ~45.86% (rural ~54.18%, urban ~36.29%). Housing: ~10.07% (urban only in combined). This high food weight makes India's CPI sensitive to food inflation.

q: The Human Development Index (HDI) measures countries on:
opts: Life expectancy, education, and income (GNI per capita)
explain: HDI (UNDP) has three dimensions: Long and healthy life (life expectancy), Knowledge (mean years + expected years of schooling), and Standard of living (GNI per capita in PPP$). Score 0 (lowest) to 1 (highest). India ranks ~134th.

q: India's 'District Primary Education Programme' (DPEP) was precursor to:
explain: DPEP (District Primary Education Programme, 1994-2002): World Bank-assisted program targeting educationally backward districts. Objectives: enroll all children in school, reduce dropout rates, improve learning outcomes, increase girls' participation. Established as pilot for universal elementary education. Succeeded by SSA (2001).

q: The term 'circular economy' refers to:
opts: An economic system that reuses and recycles instead of discarding
Economic cycle of boom and bust
Circular flow of income in national accounting
explain: Circular Economy: regenerative system that keeps resources in use for as long as possible. Principles: reduce consumption, reuse products, recycle materials, recover energy. Contrasts with linear (take-make-waste) economy. UN SDGs include circular economy elements. EU's Circular Economy Action Plan (2020). Key to achieving net-zero and sustainable development.

q: Structural unemployment is caused by:
opts: Mismatch between workers' skills and available jobs due to technological change
explain: Structural unemployment: skills mismatch due to technology changes, industry shifts, or globalization. Long-term; requires retraining. E.g., manufacturing workers displaced by automation.

q: The concept of 'disguised unemployment' is different from 'seasonal unemployment' in that:
opts: Disguised: zero marginal product; Seasonal: off-season only
explain: Disguised Unemployment (structural): workers appear employed but contribute zero output (farm has 5 workers when 3 suffice). Zero marginal product. Removing 2 workers doesn't reduce output. Seasonal Unemployment: workers unemployed part of year (farmers during off-season, tourism workers in lean season). Cyclic unemployment: due to recession. Frictional: between jobs.

q: The Public Account of India is used for transactions where the government acts as:
opts: A banker/trustee for funds not belonging to it
explain: Public Account (Article 266(2)): government acts as banker — Provident Funds, small savings, deposits. These are liabilities; Parliament's approval not needed for withdrawals.

q: The 'principal-agent problem' in economics occurs when:
opts: Agent's interests diverge from the principal's (employer's)
Government is the agent for citizens
Central bank is agent for government
Banks are agents for depositors only
explain: Principal-Agent Problem: principal (owner, shareholder) hires agent (manager, employee) but cannot perfectly monitor agent's actions. Agent may shirk, take excessive risks, or pursue own interests at principal's expense. Solutions: incentive contracts (bonuses, stock options), monitoring, reputation effects. Related: corporate governance, insurance (insurer-insured), doctor-patient.

q: The term 'stagflation' was coined during:
explain: 'Stagflation' coined by British politician Iain Macleod (1965, combined 'stagnation' + 'inflation'). Major episode: 1973-74 OPEC oil embargo quadrupled oil prices → cost-push inflation worldwide + recession (less production) → stagflation. Challenged Keynesian consensus that inflation and unemployment are inversely related (Phillips Curve). Led to Monetarism (Friedman) gaining prominence.

q: The Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana (PMUY) was launched to:
opts: Provide LPG connections to BPL households
explain: PMUY (May 2016): provided free LPG connections (deposit waived, EMI for stove/first cylinder) to BPL women. Phase 1: 5 crore connections. Phase 2: 3 crore more. PMUY 2.0 (2021): 1 crore more, including migrants. Beneficiary: women in BPL household. Benefits: reduction in indoor air pollution, time saved from collecting biomass fuel, empowerment of women.

q: The term 'PPP' (Purchasing Power Parity) is used to:
opts: Compare GDP across countries adjusting for price-level differences
explain: PPP: converts GDP using exchange rates that equalize purchasing power (prices of identical goods). Eliminates price level differences between countries for fair comparison. India's GDP at market exchange rate: ~$3.7 trillion (5th globally). At PPP: ~$13+ trillion (3rd globally after USA and China). PPP reflects actual living standards better.

q:
With reference to types of budget deficits, consider the following statements:
1. Fiscal deficit is the difference between total expenditure and total receipts excluding borrowings.
2. Revenue deficit is the excess of revenue expenditure over revenue receipts.
3. Primary deficit equals fiscal deficit minus interest payments.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
explain: All three are correct, standard budget-deficit definitions used in Indian public finance. Hence 1, 2 and 3.

q: Fiscal Federalism in India involves:
opts: Division of taxing/spending powers between Centre and States
No central government role in finance
explain: Fiscal Federalism: distribution of financial powers. Centre: income tax, corporate tax, customs, GST (shared), cess/surcharge. States: stamp duty, excise on liquor, land revenue, profession tax, entry tax (now subsumed in GST). Shared: GST (CGST to Centre, SGST to State). Finance Commission determines revenue sharing. States depend significantly on central transfers (devolution + grants).

q: Monetary policy in India is conducted by:
opts: RBI, via the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)
explain: RBI's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC): established 2016. 6 members: RBI Governor (chair), Deputy Governor (monetary policy), one RBI officer + 3 external members appointed by Central Government. Meets bimonthly. Target: CPI inflation 4% (with ±2% band). Tools: Repo Rate, Reverse Repo, SLR, CRR, Open Market Operations.

q: The Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana is meant for:
explain: Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana (2015, 'Beti Bachao Beti Padhao' initiative): post office/bank savings scheme for girl child. Features: account opened before girl turns 10, deposits up to Rs 1.5 lakh/year, ~8% interest (one of highest for small savings), tax benefits under Section 80C, withdrawal for education (50%) at age 18, maturity at 21.

q: The New Economic Policy (NEP) 1991 in India is also called:
explain: NEP 1991 (LPG): India faced forex crisis (2 weeks' reserves, credit downgrade). Finance Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh initiated: Liberalization (abolished industrial licensing for most sectors, devalued rupee), Privatization (disinvestment in PSUs, private entry in telecom, aviation, banking), Globalization (reduced import duties from ~120% avg to 25-30%, FDI policy liberalized). Transformed India's economy.

q: What is 'opportunity cost' in economics?
opts: Value of the next best alternative foregone
The actual monetary cost of a good
explain: Opportunity Cost: value of the best alternative foregone when a choice is made. Example: if you spend Rs 1 lakh on a business and it could have earned 8% in a bank (Rs 8,000), then opportunity cost = Rs 8,000/year. Fundamental to economics — every decision involves opportunity cost. Key to understanding rational decision-making.

q: India's National Monetisation Pipeline targets which assets?
explain: NMP (2021-25, Rs 6 lakh crore target): monetize operational public infrastructure by giving long-term lease/right of use to private sector. Asset categories: Roads (NHAI: Rs 1.6 lakh cr), Railways (Rs 1.5 lakh cr — freight terminals, stations, hills railways), Power (PGCIL, NTPC: Rs 0.85 lakh cr), Telecom (BSNL, BBNL), Oil & Gas (GAIL, IOCL), Airports, Ports, Stadiums, Warehouses.

q: The World Trade Organization (WTO) was established in:
explain: WTO (January 1, 1995): replaced GATT (1947) after Uruguay Round negotiations (1986-1994). HQ: Geneva, Switzerland. 164 member countries. Functions: sets and enforces global trade rules, resolves trade disputes, negotiates new trade agreements. India is a founding member. Doha Development Round (2001): stalled over agricultural subsidies.

q: Special Economic Zones (SEZs) in India offer:
opts: Tax concessions and duty-free imports for export-oriented industries
explain: SEZs: designated areas with different economic regulations to promote exports and attract investment. Benefits: duty-free import of capital goods/raw materials, income tax exemptions (sunset clauses), 100% FDI allowed, simplified labor/environmental regulations. India's first SEZ: Kandla (1965, then Asia's first export processing zone). SEZ Act 2005: rapid expansion. India has 200+ SEZs.

q:
With reference to India's flexible inflation targeting framework, consider the following statements:
1. The RBI targets CPI-based inflation at 4%, with a tolerance band of +/- 2%.
2. The target is reviewed by the government in consultation with the RBI periodically.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Both are correct — the 4% target with a +/-2% band, and periodic government-RBI review, are accurate features of India's inflation-targeting framework.

q: The National Income Accounting identity (Expenditure method) GDP = C + I + G + (X – M) where X-M is:
explain: GDP Expenditure Method: C (Private Final Consumption Expenditure, ~57% of India's GDP) + I (Gross Fixed Capital Formation/Investments, ~30%) + G (Government Final Consumption Expenditure, ~11%) + (X-M) Net Exports (~-2 to -3% for India — trade deficit). Also: Income Method and Production/Output Method give same result.

q: The External Commercial Borrowings (ECB) framework allows Indian companies to borrow from:
opts: Foreign lenders (banks, bond markets) in foreign currency
Government of India through special bonds
explain: ECB: foreign currency loans raised by Indian corporates from foreign lenders (recognized lenders like foreign banks, foreign bondholders). Regulated by RBI under FEMA. Used to access cheaper foreign funds.

q: The Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme was introduced to:
opts: Boost domestic manufacturing via incentives on incremental sales
explain: PLI Scheme (2020-21): government gives manufacturers financial incentives (3-5% of incremental production over a base year) to boost domestic manufacturing. Initially 13 sectors: mobile phones (Apple, Samsung set up factories), pharmaceuticals (API), automobiles, textiles, food processing, etc. Aims to make India a global manufacturing hub.

q: India's first stock exchange was:
explain: Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE, 1875): Asia's oldest stock exchange. Started informally in 1855 under a banyan tree, formalized as 'The Native Share and Stock Brokers' Association.' Moved to Dalal Street, Mumbai. India's second oldest exchange: Ahmedabad Stock Exchange (1894). Calcutta Stock Exchange: 1908. Madras Stock Exchange: 1937.
