q: A Giffen good is one where demand increases as price increases because:
opts: It has high brand value (Veblen effect)
It is an inferior good where the income effect dominates the substitution effect
explain: Giffen goods (Robert Giffen): inferior goods where price rise reduces real income so severely that consumers buy more (cannot afford the superior substitute). Classic example: bread in 19th-century England.

q: The WTO (World Trade Organisation) replaced which organisation?
opts: GATT (General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade)
explain: WTO replaced GATT on 1 January 1995. It administers multilateral trade agreements and provides a forum for trade negotiations and dispute resolution.

q: Which index measures the inequality of income or wealth distribution in a country?
explain: Gini Coefficient (Corrado Gini, 1912): 0 = perfect equality; 1 = maximum inequality. Derived from Lorenz Curve. India's Gini ~0.36 (income). Used alongside HDI to measure inclusive development.

q: India's Sovereign Wealth Fund equivalent is:
explain: NIIF (2015): India's quasi-sovereign wealth fund. Government of India owns 49%, remaining 51% from institutional investors (ADIA of Abu Dhabi, CDPQ of Canada, etc.). Invests in infrastructure assets.

q: The Marginal Propensity to Save (MPS) + Marginal Propensity to Consume (MPC) always equals:
explain: MPC + MPS = 1 (an additional unit of income is either consumed or saved, nothing else). Investment Multiplier k = 1/(1−MPC) = 1/MPS. Higher MPC → higher multiplier effect of government spending.

q:
With reference to Gross Value Added (GVA), consider the following statements:
1. GVA measures the value of output less the value of intermediate consumption.
2. GDP at market prices equals GVA plus taxes on products minus subsidies on products.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Both are correct, standard national accounting relationships used since India's 2015 GVA-based methodology revision.

q: Export-Import Bank of India (EXIM Bank) was established to:
opts: Finance and facilitate India's international trade
explain: EXIM Bank (Export-Import Bank of India, 1982, HQ Mumbai): fully government-owned. Functions: long-term export credit to foreign buyers of Indian goods (buyer's credit), supplier's credit to Indian exporters, project export finance, overseas investment finance, and Lines of Credit to foreign governments for import of Indian goods.

q: The Wholesale Price Index (WPI) in India measures:
explain: WPI: measures average change in prices of goods at first point of bulk sale (wholesale). Base year: 2011-12. Three groups: Primary Articles (22.6% weight — food, non-food, minerals), Fuel & Power (13.2%), Manufactured Products (64.2%). WPI has been replaced by CPI as India's headline inflation indicator (since 2014). WPI useful for PPI (Producer Price Index) analysis.

q: Reverse Repo Rate is:
opts: Rate at which banks borrow from RBI
Rate at which RBI borrows from commercial banks (absorbs excess liquidity)
Rate at which banks lend to NBFCs
explain: Reverse Repo Rate: The rate at which RBI borrows from commercial banks. When banks park excess funds with RBI at reverse repo rate, it reduces money supply (liquidity absorption). Reverse repo < Repo rate.

q: India's National Pension System (NPS) is regulated by:
opts: Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA)
explain: NPS regulated by PFRDA (Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority), established under PFRDA Act 2013. NPS launched 2004 for government employees (replaced old pension). Extended to all citizens 2009.

q: The 'trickle-down' and 'inclusive growth' debate centers on:
opts: Whether growth alone reduces poverty or needs redistribution
explain: Growth-Poverty nexus: Growth is necessary (expands economic pie, creates jobs) but not sufficient (poor may not benefit if inequality rises). Evidence: some growth episodes increased inequality (India post-1991). Inclusive growth policies: social safety nets (MGNREGA), human capital investment (education, health), progressive taxation, financial inclusion. UN SDG 10: reduce inequality.

q: The term 'money supply' (M3) in India includes:
opts: Currency in circulation + demand deposits + time deposits with banks — M3 is the broadest measure ('broad money') used by RBI
Only paper currency and coins (that's M0/reserve money)
explain: RBI's money supply measures: M0 (reserve money/monetary base): currency in circulation + bankers' deposits with RBI. M1 (narrow money): M0 + demand deposits. M2: M1 + savings deposits with post offices. M3 (broad money): M1 + net time deposits with banks — the main measure used for monetary policy. M4: M3 + all post office deposits.

q: The PM-KISAN (Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi) scheme provides:
opts: Rs 6,000/year directly to farmer families' bank accounts
explain: PM-KISAN (December 2018): income support of Rs 6,000/year in 3 installments of Rs 2,000 each to all farmer families (initially small/marginal, then extended to all landholding farmers). Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) to Aadhaar-linked bank accounts. About 9 crore+ beneficiaries. Annual expenditure: ~Rs 60,000 crore.

q: India's largest source of tax revenue to the central government is:
explain: India's tax revenue structure: Total taxes: GST (largest indirect tax) + Income tax (direct tax). Within direct taxes: corporate tax ~53%, personal income tax ~47%. GST revenues: ~Rs 1.6 lakh crore/month (2023-24). Customs duty: on imports. India's tax-GDP ratio: ~11%, lower than OECD average (~34%).

q: The term 'agflation' was coined during:
explain: Agflation: price surge driven by agricultural commodity prices (food inflation). 2007-08 food crisis: wheat prices rose 130%, rice 74%, corn 56%. Causes: biofuel mandates (US corn for ethanol), droughts in Australia/Ukraine, export bans (India, Vietnam, Egypt for rice), financial speculators in commodity markets. Affected food security of poor countries most.

q: India's 'Ease of Doing Business' ranking has been assessed by:
explain: World Bank's Doing Business Report (1990-2021): ranked countries on business regulations (starting business, getting credit, paying taxes, enforcing contracts, etc.). India rose from 142 (2014) to 63 (2020) — dramatic improvement. Report discontinued in 2021 due to data manipulation allegations. World Bank now developing new Business Ready (B-READY) report.

q: Pension reforms in India were initiated with the establishment of:
opts: PFRDA (Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority)
explain: PFRDA (Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority): interim PFRDA set up 2003 to manage NPS rollout for new central government employees. PFRDA Act 2013 (in force 2014) gave it statutory status. Regulates: NPS (National Pension System — for government and private sector), APY (Atal Pension Yojana — for unorganized sector). Fund managers: SBI, LIC, HDFC, ICICI Prudential, Kotak, UTI, Aditya Birla.

q: The term 'Repo Rate' versus 'Reverse Repo Rate' can be understood as:
opts: Repo: banks borrow from RBI; Reverse Repo: RBI borrows from banks
Repo is lower than Reverse Repo
Only one of these is used by RBI
explain: Repo Rate: banks need short-term funds → sell G-Secs to RBI with agreement to repurchase → RBI charges repo rate. Reverse Repo: banks have excess funds → park with RBI (RBI issues securities or gives written promise) → RBI pays reverse repo rate. Reverse Repo < Repo (currently Repo - 0.25%). Corridor: Reverse Repo (floor) to MSF (Marginal Standing Facility, Repo + 0.25%, ceiling).

q: The National Income of India is measured at:
explain: India's National Accounts use two price concepts: (1) Market prices: actual prices including indirect taxes (GST, excise) minus subsidies. (2) Basic prices: market prices excluding product taxes + product subsidies. (3) Factor cost: basic prices minus production taxes + production subsidies. GDP at market prices is commonly cited for international comparison.

q:
Consider the following statements about labour law reforms in India:
1. The government has consolidated numerous central labour laws into a smaller set of Labour Codes.
2. The Labour Codes cover areas such as wages, industrial relations, social security and occupational safety.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Both are correct — India consolidated numerous central labour laws into four Labour Codes covering these areas.

q:
With reference to the Minimum Support Price (MSP) mechanism, consider the following statements:
1. MSP is recommended by the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP).
2. The Food Corporation of India (FCI) is the nodal agency for MSP-based procurement of cereals.
3. MSP guarantees a minimum price only for crops sold to private traders, not government agencies.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
explain: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is incorrect — MSP is precisely the price at which government agencies (like FCI) procure crops from farmers; it doesn't govern private trader transactions. Hence 1 and 2 only.

q: India's National Accounts are compiled using which base year?
explain: India's National Accounts base year revision: 2004-05 → 2011-12 (January 2015). Changes: MCA21 database (corporate sector), better coverage of financial services, improved price deflators, GVA (Gross Value Added) reported at basic prices instead of factor cost. Revision made India's GDP estimates higher than earlier (better coverage of organized sector).

q: India's Merchandise Exports have the following major categories:
opts: Engineering goods, petroleum, gems & jewellery, chemicals, textiles
explain: India's top merchandise export categories: Engineering goods (machinery, electronics, metal products), Petroleum products (refined petroleum), Gems and Jewellery (cut diamonds, gold jewellery), Chemicals and pharmaceuticals, Textiles and apparel. Services exports are separate and even larger: IT/ITES (~$250 billion). Total merchandise exports: ~$450 billion; services: ~$250+ billion.

q:
Consider the following statements about crop insurance in India:
1. Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) provides insurance coverage against crop loss due to natural calamities.
2. Premium rates paid by farmers under PMFBY are subsidised, with the government bearing a large share of the actuarial premium.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Both are correct — PMFBY covers natural-calamity crop losses, and farmer premiums are kept low with the government subsidising the remainder.

q: The Swachh Bharat Mission (Urban) 2.0 focuses on:
opts: Making cities garbage-free with waste management, wastewater treatment
explain: SBM-Urban 2.0 (launched October 1, 2021): garbage-free cities, waste management (dry/wet/hazardous segregation), used water management (UWM), remediation of legacy dump sites. SBM-U 1.0 focused on ODF.

q: The concept of 'transfer payments' in national accounting includes:
opts: Govt payments with no goods/services in return
explain: Transfer Payments: one-way payment with no corresponding output — included in government budget but NOT in GDP calculation. Examples: pensions, unemployment benefits, scholarships, welfare payments, food subsidies. These transfer purchasing power from government to beneficiaries but don't create new output. Included in recipients' income but not in GDP via expenditure method.

q: Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) were established under:
explain: RRBs (1975/1976): established to provide banking services in rural areas (disadvantaged by cooperative banks' limitations). First RRB: Prathama Grameen Bank (Moradabad, 1975). Ownership: Centre 50%, State 15%, Sponsor Bank 35%. RBI Governor's advice: each district should have an RRB. Now consolidated: 43 RRBs (from 196 originally). Regulated by NABARD.

q: India's first Five Year Plan (1951-56) primarily focused on:
opts: Agricultural development and rehabilitation of refugees
explain: First FYP (1951-56): Harrod-Domar model; focus on agriculture (after 1943 Bengal famine memories), power, transport, rehabilitation of 1947 partition refugees. Bhakra Nangal dam a key project. Exceeded growth targets.

q: Priority Sector Lending (PSL) requires Indian commercial banks to lend what percentage of ANBC to priority sectors?
explain: PSL target: 40% of Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC) for domestic scheduled commercial banks. Priority sectors: Agriculture (18%), MSMEs, Education, Housing, Weaker Sections (10%).

q:
Consider the following statements on causes of inflation:
1. Demand-pull inflation occurs when aggregate demand exceeds aggregate supply in the economy.
2. Cost-push inflation results from rising input costs (e.g., wages, raw materials) being passed on to consumers.
3. An increase in money supply, unmatched by output growth, can also contribute to inflation.
4. Inflation, once it begins, cannot be influenced by monetary policy tools.
How many of the above statements are correct?
explain: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is incorrect — monetary policy (repo rate, CRR etc.) is precisely one of the main tools used to influence and control inflation. Hence only three.

q: The Union Budget is prepared by which Ministry?
explain: Union Budget preparation: Ministry of Finance (DEA — Budget Division) issues budget circular to all ministries for expenditure estimates; Department of Revenue handles tax proposals (Direct Tax: CBDT, Indirect Tax: CBIC). Finance Minister consults stakeholders, states, industry. Finance Bill (tax changes) + Appropriation Bill (expenditure) presented together.

q: The 'Kuznets Curve' on income inequality suggests:
opts: Inequality first rises then falls with development (inverted U)
No relationship between inequality and development
explain: Kuznets Curve (Simon Kuznets, Nobel 1971): inequality vs per capita income forms an inverted U. Early development: inequality rises (structural shift, unequal gains). Later: inequality falls (education spreads, welfare state, minimum wages, service economy). Critics: doesn't apply universally (Latin America stayed unequal; China/East Asia grew with initially low inequality). Environment Kuznets Curve: similar pattern for pollution.

q: The Neyveli Lignite Corporation (NLC India) is located in:
explain: NLC India (formerly Neyveli Lignite Corporation): Central PSU in Neyveli, Cuddalore district. World's largest open-cast lignite mine. Mines lignite → burns in thermal plants → generates electricity (mainly supplied to Tamil Nadu and southern states). Also has major solar power capacity. Established 1956.

q: The Banking Ombudsman Scheme provides:
opts: Free, independent complaint resolution against banks
explain: Banking Ombudsman (BO): customer can file complaint if bank doesn't resolve within 30 days. BO can award compensation up to Rs 20 lakh. RB-IOS 2021: unified scheme covering commercial banks, cooperative banks, NBFCs, and non-bank PPIs (payment instruments). Centralized receipt: complaints filed online at cms.rbi.org.in. Turnaround: 30 days resolution target.

q:
Consider the following statements regarding SLR (Statutory Liquidity Ratio):
1. SLR requires banks to maintain a minimum percentage of deposits in the form of cash, gold, or approved securities.
2. SLR funds are held with the RBI in the same manner as CRR funds.
3. A reduction in SLR frees up more funds for banks to lend.
4. SLR is fixed exclusively by the Government of India, not the RBI.
How many of the above statements are correct?
explain: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is incorrect — unlike CRR, SLR assets are held by the banks themselves, not deposited with RBI. Statement 4 is incorrect — SLR is set by the RBI under the Banking Regulation Act, not the government. Hence only two.

q: FDI stands for:
explain: FDI is an investment made by a company or individual in one country in business interests in another country. India allows FDI in most sectors under automatic and government approval routes.

q: Inflation means:
opts: Increase in the general price level
explain: Inflation is the rate at which the general price level rises, eroding purchasing power. Measured by CPI (Consumer Price Index) and WPI (Wholesale Price Index) in India.

q: The SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India) was given statutory powers in:
explain: SEBI: established 1988 as non-statutory body; given statutory powers under SEBI Act, 1992 (following Harshad Mehta scam of 1992 — manipulated stock prices using banking funds). HQ: Mumbai. Functions: regulates stock exchanges (BSE, NSE), brokers, FPIs, mutual funds, merchant banks; prevents insider trading and market manipulation.

q: Which component of Balance of Payments records foreign direct investment and portfolio investment?
explain: The Financial Account records FDI, FPI (portfolio investment), and other investment flows. The Capital Account records capital transfers and non-produced assets.

q: The Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA) is under:
explain: APEDA (1986, APEDA Act 1985, HQ New Delhi): statutory body under Commerce Ministry. Promotes and regulates export of: scheduled products (fresh fruits/vegetables, flower, processed foods, meat, poultry, dairy, cereals, etc.). Assigns registration certificate to exporters; sets quality standards; develops packaging, marketing, and infrastructure.

q: Non-Performing Assets (NPAs) are loans where:
opts: Loan overdue 90+ days on interest or principal
Bank has invested in unproductive assets
explain: NPA: loan where interest/principal is overdue for 90+ days. Classification: Substandard (NPA for <1 year), Doubtful (NPA for 1-3 years, collateral insufficient), Loss (uncollectable, to be written off). High NPAs reduce banks' profitability and ability to lend. India's NPA problem peaked ~2018 (GNPAs of ~11.2% of advances). IBC 2016 helped resolve many NPAs.

q:
Statement-I: The Green Revolution significantly boosted foodgrain production in India from the late 1960s onward.
Statement-II: It involved widespread adoption of High Yielding Variety (HYV) seeds combined with chemical fertilisers and assured irrigation.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
opts: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
explain: Both statements are correct, and the technology package described in Statement-II (HYV seeds, fertiliser, irrigation) is precisely what drove the production gains described in Statement-I.

q: Treasury Bills (T-Bills) in India are short-term government securities issued for maturities of:
explain: T-Bills: zero-coupon short-term instruments. India has 3 types: 91-day, 182-day, 364-day T-Bills. Issued at discount, redeemed at face value. Used for short-term government cash management.

q: India adopted economic liberalization in:
explain: 1991 Economic Reforms: India faced severe forex crisis (only 3 weeks' reserves), high inflation, and fiscal deficit. PM P.V. Narasimha Rao and FM Dr. Manmohan Singh introduced: dismantling License Raj, reducing import tariffs, opening FDI, devaluing rupee, privatization. Called LPG reforms. India's GDP growth accelerated post-reform.

q: Long-run economic growth is determined by:
explain: Long-run growth determinants (Robert Solow's model): capital accumulation (investment) and technological progress (total factor productivity). Endogenous growth theory (Paul Romer): knowledge, human capital, and innovation drive sustained growth. Key: education quality, R&D spending, institutions, rule of law, and infrastructure.

q: The National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) guarantees:
opts: 100 days of unskilled work per rural household per year
explain: MGNREGA (2005, implemented 2006): provides legal right to 100 days of unskilled work per household per year at minimum wage. If work not provided within 15 days, unemployment allowance paid. Works include road construction, water conservation, land development. Among world's largest social protection programs. Renamed to include Gandhi: MGNREGS.

q: The National Rural Health Mission (NHM) was launched in:
explain: NRHM (National Rural Health Mission, 2005): flagship health scheme for rural areas. Key feature: ASHA workers — trained female community health activists (one per 1000 population) who link communities with health facilities. NRHM + National Urban Health Mission merged into NHM (National Health Mission) in 2013.

q: Gold Monetization Scheme (GMS) was launched to:
opts: Mobilize idle household gold for interest
explain: Gold Monetization Scheme (2015, replaced GDS 1999): households and institutions deposit physical gold (minimum 10 grams) with banks. Earn interest (2.25-2.50% p.a.) + get back gold or equivalent value. Banks can lend to jewellers or sell. Aims to reduce India's gold imports (~800-900 tonnes/year) by mobilizing India's estimated 25,000 tonnes of privately held gold.

q: The 'Golden Quadrilateral' is:
explain: Golden Quadrilateral (NHDP Phase 1): 4-6 lane highways connecting Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, and Kolkata. Total: 5,846 km. Developed by NHAI under National Highway Development Project (Phase 1, 2001). Substantially completed by 2012. Connected India's largest economic centers; greatly reduced transport time. Also 'North-South and East-West Corridor' connecting Srinagar-Kanyakumari and Porbandar-Silchar.

q: The CRR (Cash Reserve Ratio) means:
opts: The percentage of deposits banks must lend to industry
The minimum percentage of deposits banks must maintain as cash with RBI
The ratio of gold to currency
The minimum capital banks must hold
explain: CRR is the percentage of a bank's total deposits that must be maintained as cash reserves with the RBI. It controls money supply — higher CRR = less money available to lend.

q: The Economic Survey is presented in Parliament just before the Union Budget by:
opts: Chief Economic Adviser to the Government of India
explain: Economic Survey: prepared by the Economic Division of Ministry of Finance under the Chief Economic Adviser (CEA). Reviews the economy's performance. Presented before Union Budget. Volume 1: thematic; Volume 2: data.

q: Deadweight loss in economics refers to:
opts: Loss of economic efficiency when equilibrium is not achieved (lost surplus)
explain: Deadweight loss: reduction in total surplus (consumer + producer) due to market inefficiency caused by taxes, price controls, monopoly, or externalities. Represents foregone transactions.

q:
With reference to poverty measurement in India, consider the following statements:
1. The Tendulkar Committee revised the poverty line methodology, moving away from a calorie-based norm.
2. The Rangarajan Committee later proposed a further revised poverty line, with a higher poverty threshold than the Tendulkar line.
3. NITI Aayog has since taken up work related to poverty and multidimensional deprivation measurement, including a Multidimensional Poverty Index.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
explain: All three are correct — the Tendulkar and Rangarajan Committees' methodologies, and NITI Aayog's later Multidimensional Poverty Index work, are all real, well-documented developments in India's poverty measurement history. Hence 1, 2 and 3.

q: India is classified as a:
explain: India's mixed economy (as in the Constitution's Directive Principles): public sector controls strategic industries (defense, rail, atomic energy), while private sector operates in most areas. Since 1991 reforms, India has moved significantly toward market economy with reduced government control.

q: The NITI Aayog's 'Aspirational Districts Programme' targets:
explain: Aspirational Districts Programme (2018): 112 districts ranked on 49 indicators across 5 themes: Health & Nutrition, Education, Agriculture & Water Resources, Financial Inclusion & Skill Development, Basic Infrastructure. Real-time monitoring on Championing Change portal. 'Competitive and cooperative federalism' — districts compete and learn from each other. Success: significant improvement in health, nutrition, education indicators.

q: A futures contract obligates the buyer to purchase an asset at:
opts: Market price on the day of trading
A predetermined price on a specified future date
The lowest price in the contract period
A floating price determined at settlement
explain: Futures contract: standardized, exchange-traded obligation to buy/sell an asset at a set price on a specified future date. Both buyer and seller are obligated (unlike options, where buyer has the right).

q: India's Wholesale Price Index (WPI) is published by:
opts: Ministry of Commerce and Industry (Office of Economic Adviser)
explain: WPI: published monthly by Office of the Economic Adviser (OEA), Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), Ministry of Commerce and Industry. Base year 2011-12, 697 commodities.

q: The Ease of Doing Business (EoDB) Index was published by the World Bank under which report?
explain: World Bank's 'Doing Business Report' published EoDB rankings from 2003 to 2021 (discontinued). India improved from rank 142 (2014) to 63 (2019). Report discontinued after data integrity concerns.

q: RBI acts as the 'Lender of Last Resort' which means:
opts: It lends to the government only
It provides emergency liquidity to banks facing temporary shortages to prevent systemic collapse
It is the last bank to make profits
It lends to countries in balance of payments crisis
explain: Lender of Last Resort: RBI provides emergency credit to solvent but illiquid banks to prevent bank runs and financial crises. This function was conceptualized by Walter Bagehot (1873).

q:
Consider the following statements about Special Economic Zones (SEZs) in India:
1. SEZs are designated duty-free enclaves treated as foreign territory for trade and tariff purposes.
2. Units within SEZs typically enjoy tax incentives and simplified regulatory compliance.
3. The SEZ Act was passed in India in 2005.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
explain: All three are correct — standard facts about India's SEZ policy (Act passed 2005, duty-free enclave treatment, tax/regulatory incentives). Hence 1, 2 and 3.

q:
Statement-I: Inflation erodes the purchasing power of money over time.
Statement-II: As the general price level rises, a fixed amount of money can buy fewer goods and services than before.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
opts: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
explain: Both statements are correct, and Statement-II is a direct, textbook explanation of the mechanism described in Statement-I.

q: The Participatory Notes (P-Notes) are:
opts: Instruments FPIs issue to unregistered overseas investors
explain: Participatory Notes (P-Notes or ODIs — Offshore Derivative Instruments): FPIs registered with SEBI issue P-Notes to foreign investors (who may not want direct SEBI registration). Allows anonymous investment in Indian markets. SEBI has tightened P-Note regulations (2017): disclosure of beneficial owner required. P-Note exposure reduced from ~50% to ~3-5% of total FPI holdings.

q: The Finance Commission of India, constituted every five years under Article 280, primarily recommends the distribution of which of the following?
opts: Net proceeds of taxes between the Union and the States
explain: The Finance Commission recommends the distribution of the net proceeds of taxes between the Union and the States, and among the States themselves.

q:
With reference to national income accounting, consider the following statements:
1. GDP measures the value of final goods and services produced within a country's domestic territory in a given period.
2. GNP includes net factor income from abroad, unlike GDP.
3. Net National Product (NNP) is calculated as GNP minus depreciation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
explain: All three are correct, standard national income accounting definitions. Hence 1, 2 and 3.

q: Keynesian economics advocates that during recession:
opts: Government should cut spending and raise taxes (austerity)
Government should increase spending and cut taxes to stimulate aggregate demand (expansionary fiscal policy)
Central bank should tighten money supply
explain: Keynes argued that during recession, private sector demand collapses, so government must fill the gap through expansionary fiscal policy — increased spending (even deficit spending/pump priming) and tax cuts. This was used in the 2008-09 global financial crisis.

q: Tamil Nadu's economy is ranked among Indian states by GSDP (Gross State Domestic Product) as:
explain: Tamil Nadu: GSDP ~Rs 25+ lakh crore (2023-24), consistently among top 3 states (Maharashtra is typically 1st). TN contributes significantly to: auto manufacturing (Chennai = Detroit of India), textiles (Tirupur knit capital), leather (Vellore), IT (Chennai, Coimbatore), and tourism.

q: The term 'moral hazard' in economics refers to:
opts: Taking more risk because one is shielded from the consequences
explain: Moral hazard: tendency to take on more risk when protected from the consequences (risk is transferred to another party). Examples: bank risky lending (expecting government bailout — 'too big to fail'), insured driving recklessly, principal-agent problem (employee working less hard without monitoring). Key concept in insurance economics, banking regulation.

q: The index 'Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI)' measures poverty using:
explain: MPI (UNDP and OPHI — Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative): multidimensional poverty measure using 10 indicators across 3 dimensions. A household is 'deprived' in each indicator; 'multidimensionally poor' if deprived in >33% of weighted indicators. India's MPI: 415 million exited poverty 2005-06 to 2019-21 (massive reduction). India publishes National MPI annually.

q: 'Market failure' occurs when:
opts: Free markets fail to allocate resources efficiently
explain: Market Failure: situations where free markets don't achieve Pareto efficiency. Types: (1) Externalities (pollution, education spillovers), (2) Public goods (non-excludable, non-rival: defence, lighthouses), (3) Information asymmetry (adverse selection, moral hazard), (4) Market power (monopoly), (5) Missing markets (insurance for some risks). Government intervention: taxes, subsidies, regulation, direct provision.

q: Which RBI instrument provides short-term liquidity adjustment, where banks park excess funds with RBI overnight?
explain: Reverse Repo: banks park excess funds with RBI overnight and earn interest (currently Repo − 25 bps = SDF rate). Repo: banks borrow from RBI against G-Secs. Together they form the LAF corridor.

q: The concept of 'Creative Destruction' associated with Joseph Schumpeter describes:
opts: Innovation that destroys existing industries while creating new ones, driving capitalist progress
explain: Schumpeter's Creative Destruction: innovation (new products, methods, markets) makes existing industries obsolete, destroying old capital while creating new. Key driver of long-run capitalist dynamism. (E.g., smartphones destroyed film cameras.)

q: What is 'stagflation' and when was it first observed?
opts: Simultaneous stagnation and inflation, first seen in the 1970s oil crisis
explain: Stagflation: simultaneous recession and inflation. Phillips Curve (1958): inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment (when inflation is high, unemployment is low). 1973 OPEC oil embargo: oil prices quadrupled → cost-push inflation PLUS economic recession → stagflation (high inflation + high unemployment simultaneously). Disproved simple Phillips Curve. Led to Monetarism (Friedman) and supply-side economics (Reagan).

q: Open Market Operations (OMO) by RBI involve:
opts: RBI buying/selling govt securities to manage liquidity
explain: OMO: primary tool of RBI's liquidity management. OMO purchase (bond purchase): RBI buys G-Secs from banks → banks get cash → more liquidity in system → lower interest rates. OMO sale: RBI sells G-Secs → banks give cash to RBI → less liquidity → higher rates. Twist OMOs: buy long-term, sell short-term bonds to control yield curve.

q: The term 'crowding out' in economics refers to:
opts: Government borrowing raises interest rates, reducing private investment
explain: Crowding Out: when government increases spending/borrowing → demands more funds from financial markets → interest rates rise → private investment becomes more expensive and falls. Classical economists worry about this effect of fiscal stimulus. Counter-argument (Keynesians): in recession, resources are underutilized, so government spending need not crowd out private investment.

q: GST (Goods and Services Tax) in India replaced which of these taxes?
opts: VAT, Service Tax, Excise Duty and other indirect taxes
explain: GST (implemented 1 July 2017) subsumed over 17 central and state indirect taxes including VAT, service tax, central excise duty, CST, entertainment tax, luxury tax, entry tax.

q: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) was established at:
explain: IMF: established at Bretton Woods, New Hampshire (July 1944), alongside World Bank. Came into existence 1945, HQ: Washington DC. Functions: balance of payments assistance, macroeconomic surveillance, technical assistance. Special Drawing Rights (SDR) is IMF's reserve currency. India's largest borrowing from IMF: 1991 crisis ($2.2 billion, mortgaged 67 tons of gold).

q: Consumer Surplus is the difference between:
opts: What consumers are willing to pay and what they actually pay
explain: Consumer Surplus = Willingness to Pay − Market Price. It represents the benefit consumers gain from buying at the market price, which is lower than their maximum willingness to pay.

q: Which body formulates India's monetary policy?
explain: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is India's central bank and formulates monetary policy to control inflation, money supply, and credit.

q: The Goods and Services Tax (GST) follows which principle?
explain: GST is destination-based: taxes collected where goods/services are finally consumed. This is why Integrated GST (IGST) on interstate trade is given to the consuming state (not the producing state). Before GST: CST (Central Sales Tax) was origin-based — producing states got revenue. GST corrects this inter-state revenue distortion.

q: Scheduled Banks in India are those listed in:
opts: Second Schedule of the RBI Act 1934
explain: Scheduled Banks: listed in 2nd Schedule of RBI Act 1934. To be listed: paid-up capital + reserves ≥ Rs 5 lakh (historical, now effectively much higher). Benefits: can borrow from RBI, become member of clearinghouse. Non-scheduled banks: some cooperative banks. All public/private/foreign/SFBs/payment banks are scheduled.

q: The Global Innovation Index (GII) is published jointly by:
explain: GII published by WIPO (World Intellectual Property Organization), INSEAD, and Cornell University. Ranks economies on innovation inputs and outputs. India has improved significantly (from rank 81 in 2015 to 39 in 2023).

q: The Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) is conducted by:
explain: Annual Survey of Industries (ASI): mandatory survey of registered factories (registered under Factories Act: establishments with 10+ workers using power, or 20+ workers without power). Collects: employment, wages, input costs, output value, capital investment, fuel use. ASI data used for: IIP compilation, GDP estimates, industrial policy. Conducted annually by NSO/MoSPI.

q: The economic concept 'invisible hand' was given by:
explain: Adam Smith's 'invisible hand': when individuals act in their own self-interest (profit motive) in competitive markets, they are guided as if by an 'invisible hand' to produce goods/services society wants at efficient prices. Basis of free-market capitalism. Wealth of Nations (1776) also argued for division of labor, free trade, and against mercantilism.

q: The G20 group comprises:
explain: G20: Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Canada, China, France, Germany, India, Indonesia, Italy, Japan, Mexico, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa, South Korea, Turkey, UK, USA + EU. India held G20 presidency 2023 (September summit in New Delhi). G7 (wealthy democracies) is a subset. G20 deals with global financial stability, trade, climate, development.

q: India became a member of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank in:
explain: India joined IMF and World Bank (IBRD) in 1945. Both institutions were created at Bretton Woods Conference (July 1944) in New Hampshire, USA. IMF: financial stability; World Bank: development loans.

q: Pradhan Mantri Vaya Vandana Yojana (PMVVY) is:
explain: PMVVY (2017, LIC): pension scheme for senior citizens 60+ providing guaranteed 8% (now ~7.4%) interest for 10 years. Maximum investment: Rs 15 lakh (for Rs 10,000/month pension). Interest paid monthly/quarterly/half-yearly/annually. On maturity, principal returned. 100% government guaranteed through LIC. Tax benefit under Section 80TTB.

q: India's Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog in January 2015 with a change in focus from:
opts: Central planning to policy advisory and cooperative federalism
Five year plans to annual plans
explain: Planning Commission (1950-2014): top-down central planning, resource allocation to states. NITI Aayog (Jan 1, 2015): policy think-tank, cooperative federalism, no fund-allocation power. PM is its chairman.

q: The Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyan package announced in May 2020 was worth approximately:
explain: Aatmanirbhar Bharat: Rs 20 lakh crore package (~10% of GDP) announced in 5 tranches by Finance Minister in May 2020. Covered MSMEs, agriculture, migrant workers, education, health, structural reforms.

q: The Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) requires banks to:
opts: Hold a share of deposits in liquid assets (cash, gold, govt securities)
Keep a minimum balance with other banks
explain: SLR: banks must hold a minimum % of their deposits (NDTL) in liquid assets: cash, gold, and approved securities (mainly government bonds). Current SLR: 18% (2024). This ensures banks always have liquid assets to meet customer demands. SLR also channels funds to government borrowing. SLR + CRR together limit banks' funds available for lending.

q: India's forex reserves are managed by:
explain: RBI manages India's foreign exchange reserves (~$640-650 billion as of 2024): includes foreign currency assets (FCAs), gold, SDRs, reserve tranche with IMF. Under FEMA 1999. 4th largest globally.

q: India's GIFT City (Gujarat International Finance Tec-City) is:
opts: India's first International Financial Services Centre (IFSC)
explain: GIFT City (Gujarat International Finance Tec-City, Gandhinagar): India's first operational greenfield smart city (since 2015). Hosts GIFT IFSC (International Financial Services Centre) — India's offshore financial centre. Services: banking (foreign currency), capital markets, insurance, fund management, forex trading. Regulated by IFSCA (International Financial Services Centres Authority, 2020). Competes with DIFC (Dubai), Singapore MAS.

q:
Consider the following statements on sectoral composition of India's GDP:
1. The services sector currently contributes the largest share to India's GDP.
2. The share of agriculture in GDP has declined over the decades since independence, even though it still employs a large workforce share.
3. Industry's share of GDP has historically exceeded that of services since the 1991 reforms.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
explain: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is incorrect — services, not industry, has been the largest and fastest-growing GDP contributor since the 1990s reforms. Hence 1 and 2 only.

q: The White Revolution in India refers to:
opts: Operation Flood (milk production boom led by Verghese Kurien)
explain: White Revolution/Operation Flood: Dr. Verghese Kurien (NDDB — National Dairy Development Board) set up milk cooperatives (AMUL model) to eliminate middlemen, give fair price to farmers, and collect/process milk efficiently. India became world's largest milk producer. AMUL started in Anand, Gujarat, 1946.

q: The Human Development Index (HDI) was developed by:
explain: HDI (1990): developed by economist Mahbub ul Haq and Amartya Sen for UNDP. Composite index measuring: Life Expectancy (health), Mean/Expected Years of Schooling (education), and GNI per capita (income). HDI ranges 0-1. India's HDI rank: 134 out of 193 (UNDP 2023 report). Norway consistently tops HDI.

q: The Atal Innovation Mission (AIM) was established under:
explain: AIM (2016, under NITI Aayog): flagship initiative to promote innovation. Key programs: Atal Tinkering Labs (ATLs) — maker spaces in schools (Grades 6-12) with 3D printers, robotics kits, etc. Atal Incubation Centres (AICs): support startups. Atal Community Innovation Centres (ACICs): tier-2/3 cities and rural areas.

q: The Soil Health Card scheme launched in 2015 aims to:
opts: Provide farmers with soil nutrient status and fertilizer recommendations
explain: Soil Health Card: issued every 2 years to farmers; provides information on 12 parameters (N, P, K, pH, micronutrients) with crop-wise recommendations to optimize fertilizer use.

q: The 'production credit' versus 'investment credit' in agricultural finance:
opts: Production credit: short-term; Investment credit: long-term
Investment credit is not available in India
Production credit only exists in India
explain: Agricultural credit types: Short-term/production credit: crop loans for seasonal inputs (seeds, fertilizers, pesticides, labour) — via KCC, cooperative banks, MFIs. Long-term/investment credit: land development, irrigation installation, tractors, farm machinery, orchards — 3-7 years. NABARD refinances both types through banks and cooperatives.

q: The Bharat Net project aims to:
opts: Provide broadband connectivity to all Gram Panchayats
explain: BharatNet (2011, earlier NOFN — National Optical Fibre Network): world's largest rural broadband connectivity project. Connects all 2.5 lakh gram panchayats with optical fiber (OFC). Implemented by BSNL through state governments. Enables: e-governance, telemedicine, e-education, e-commerce in rural India. Essential backbone for Digital India.

q: Convertibility of rupee means:
opts: Full current account convertibility; partial capital account
Rupee can be exchanged for gold
explain: Current Account Convertibility (India since 1994): rupee freely convertible for: trade in goods, services, factor income payments. Capital Account Convertibility: free movement of financial capital (equity, bonds, loans). India has partial CAC: FDI (nearly full), FPI (with limits), ECBs (with RBI approval), NRI deposits. Full CAC: not yet (risk of capital flight in crises). Tarapore Committee reports (1997, 2006) on CAC.

q: India's economic growth rate (GDP growth) is measured by:
explain: National Statistical Office (NSO, formerly CSO) under Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) compiles India's national accounts (GDP data). Current base year: 2011-12. GDP growth rate: ~7% in recent years (one of fastest growing major economies). IMF, World Bank provide their own GDP estimates.

q: The term 'Current Account' in Balance of Payments includes:
opts: Trade in goods and services, primary and secondary income
explain: Current Account (CA) = Merchandise trade (visible trade) + Services trade (invisible trade: IT, tourism, shipping) + Primary Income (factor income: wages, profits, dividends, interest) + Secondary Income (current transfers: remittances, government grants). India's CA deficit largely reflects merchandise trade deficit (imports > exports), partially offset by services surplus and remittances.

q:
Statement-I: India shifted its GDP base year from 2004-05 to 2011-12 in the 2015 methodology revision.
Statement-II: The revision also moved India's national accounts from a factor-cost basis to a GVA-at-basic-prices basis, aligning better with international (UN System of National Accounts) standards.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
opts: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
explain: Both statements are correct facts about the 2015 GDP methodology revision, but they describe two separate, parallel changes (base year shift and accounting-basis shift) rather than one explaining the other.

q: Which committee recommended the rationalization of centrally sponsored schemes (CSS) in India?
explain: B.K. Chaturvedi Committee (2011): recommended rationalizing and restructuring CSS. Later, Sub-Group of CMs under CM Shivraj Singh Chouhan (2015) recommended reducing CSS from 66 to 28 for more flexibility.

q: The concept of 'Inclusive Growth' as India's official growth strategy was emphasized prominently in which Five Year Plan?
explain: 11th Five Year Plan (2007-12): 'Towards Faster and More Inclusive Growth' was its theme. Included social sector targets: education, health, women empowerment, infrastructure alongside GDP growth.

q: The Sansad TV (earlier Rajya Sabha TV + Lok Sabha TV merged) and its role in India's democracy is:
explain: Sansad TV (2021, merger of Lok Sabha TV and Rajya Sabha TV): 24/7 parliamentary television. Functions: live telecast of both Houses' proceedings, select committee meetings, budget speech; educational content (legislation, governance, history). Free-to-air on DD Free Dish and cable. Promotes parliamentary transparency.

q: What is the primary objective of the Competition Commission of India (CCI)?
opts: Preventing anti-competitive practices and promoting market competition
explain: CCI (est. 2003, operational 2009): statutory body under Competition Act 2002. Prevents anti-competitive agreements, abuses of dominant position, and regulates mergers/acquisitions to protect consumer interest.

q:
Consider the following statements regarding the Goods and Services Tax Council:
1. It is a constitutional body established under Article 279A.
2. It comprises the Union Finance Minister as Chairperson and Finance Ministers of all states as members.
3. Its recommendations on GST rates and rules are legally binding on both the Union and states without exception.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
explain: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is incorrect — the Supreme Court (2022, Mohit Minerals case) held that GST Council recommendations are persuasive, not absolutely binding, on the Union and states. Hence 1 and 2 only.

q: The Pradhan Mantri Poshan Shakti Nirman (PM POSHAN) scheme, earlier known as:
opts: ICDS (Integrated Child Development Services, for 0-6 age group)
explain: PM POSHAN (renamed from Mid-Day Meal Scheme 2021): provides one hot meal per school day to 11.8 crore students in Classes I-VIII in government/government-aided schools. Benefits: attendance ↑ (incentive), dropout ↓, nutrition ↑, social equity (reduces caste discrimination around food). One of world's largest feeding programs. Annual budget: ~Rs 12,000 crore.

q: Digital India mission aims to:
opts: Transform India into a digitally empowered society
explain: Digital India (2015): three pillars: (1) Digital Infrastructure (broadband highways, mobile connectivity, public internet access, eGovernance) (2) Digital Services (DigiLocker, e-Hospitals, e-Education, BHIM-UPI payments, Aadhaar) (3) Digital Literacy (PMGDISHA). India now has 900+ million internet users.

q: The term 'dumping' in international trade means:
opts: Exporting goods below production/domestic cost to a foreign market
Selling goods at higher price abroad
explain: Dumping: selling exported goods below cost of production (or below home market price) to gain market share in foreign country. Damages domestic industries in the importing country. WTO's Anti-Dumping Agreement: allows importing country to impose anti-dumping duties to offset price difference. India frequently imposes anti-dumping duties on Chinese goods.

q: A price floor is effective (binding) only when it is set:
explain: Price floor (minimum price) is binding only above equilibrium price, creating a surplus (supply > demand). E.g., MSP set above market price creates surplus procurement. Below equilibrium = non-binding.

q: NABARD's Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF) provides loans to:
opts: State governments for rural infrastructure projects
Commercial banks for priority sector shortfall
explain: RIDF: state governments and state-owned corporations borrow from NABARD to build rural infrastructure (roads, bridges, irrigation). Funded by shortfall in banks' PSL targets.

q: The Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Grameen Kaushalya Yojana (DDU-GKY) is:
opts: Skill training and placement for rural poor youth
explain: DDU-GKY (2014, renamed Aajeevika Skills/NRLM Skills): targets rural BPL youth. Free skill training, boarding, lodging during training, and placement assistance. Coverage: 15-35 years (extended to 45 for some groups). Target: place 75%+ trained youth in paid jobs. Implemented by Ministry of Rural Development through State Rural Livelihoods Missions.

q: The Goods and Services Tax Network (GSTN) is a:
opts: Government department under Ministry of Finance
Non-government, not-for-profit private company providing IT backbone for GST
explain: GSTN: non-government, not-for-profit company (Section 8). Provides IT infrastructure for GST registration, return filing, and tax payment. Government holds 50% (Centre 24.5% + States 24.5%), rest by PSBs/financial institutions.

q: The Wholesale Price Index (WPI) in India has a base year of:
explain: WPI base year revised to 2011-12 (released in May 2017) from 2004-05. Coverage: 697 commodities (vs 676 earlier). Weight: Primary Articles 22.62% (food: 15.26%, non-food: 4.29%, minerals: 3.07%), Fuel & Power 13.15%, Manufactured Products 64.23%. Released by Office of Economic Adviser (Ministry of Commerce). 14-day lag (faster than CPI's 12-day lag).

q: The National Food Security Act (NFSA) 2013 provides:
opts: Subsidized food grains to about 81 crore beneficiaries
explain: NFSA 2013: legal entitlement to subsidized food. Priority households: 5 kg/person/month. Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY — poorest of poor): 35 kg/household/month. Prices: rice Rs 3, wheat Rs 2, coarse cereals Rs 1 per kg. Implemented through PDS. About 81 crore people covered.

q: India's 'Unified Portal for Agricultural Statistics' (UPAg) was launched to:
opts: Provide real-time agricultural statistics on one platform
explain: UPAg (2022, Ministry of Agriculture): first-of-its-kind single platform integrating agricultural statistics from multiple agencies. Data: crop sowing/area, production, trade, price (wholesale, retail, MSP), input costs, import/export. Makes data accessible to farmers via mobile app. Aims to improve crop planning and reduce information asymmetry.

q: India's economic liberalisation was initiated in:
explain: India adopted LPG (Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation) reforms in 1991 under PM Narasimha Rao and FM Manmohan Singh, triggered by a balance of payments crisis.

q:
Consider the following statements regarding measurement of national income:
1. The value-added method avoids the problem of double counting.
2. The income method sums up factor incomes (rent, wages, interest, profit) earned by residents.
3. Real GDP is measured using current market prices, while nominal GDP uses constant base-year prices.
4. India's base year for national accounts has been revised more than once since independence.
How many of the above statements are correct?
explain: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. Statement 3 is reversed — real GDP uses constant base-year prices, while nominal GDP uses current market prices. Hence only three.

q: India's 'Integrated Goods and Services Tax' (IGST) applies to:
opts: Inter-state supply of goods/services and imports
explain: GST types: CGST (Central GST): intra-state, Centre's share. SGST (State GST): intra-state, State's share. IGST (Integrated GST): inter-state supply + imports — collected by Centre, then SGST portion transferred to consuming state. Mechanism: prevents tax cascading on inter-state trade and resolves origin-vs-destination revenue debate. Input tax credit (ITC) flows seamlessly across CGST-IGST-SGST.

q: The National Pension System (NPS) investment options include:
opts: Active Choice (self-allocated) and Auto Choice (lifecycle fund)
explain: NPS Investment Options: (1) Active Choice: subscriber allocates among E (Equity: up to 75% for private sector), C (Corporate Bonds), G (Govt Securities), A (Alternative Assets: up to 5%). (2) Auto Choice/Lifecycle Fund: equity allocation high when young (75%), automatically decreases with age. Three auto lifecycle funds: LC75 (aggressive), LC50 (moderate), LC25 (conservative).

q: NITI Aayog replaced which institution in 2015?
explain: NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015. It is a policy think-tank with a 'bottom-up' approach, unlike the top-down Five Year Plans of the Planning Commission.

q:
With reference to Non-Performing Assets (NPAs), consider the following statements:
1. A loan is generally classified as an NPA when interest or principal repayment remains overdue for a specified period (commonly 90 days).
2. High NPAs reduce a bank's ability to extend fresh credit.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Both are correct — the 90-day overdue norm is the standard NPA classification criterion, and high NPAs constrain banks' lending capacity by tying up capital in provisioning.

q: Green GDP adjusts conventional GDP by:
opts: Subtracting environmental degradation and depletion of natural resources
explain: Green GDP = GDP − Cost of environmental degradation (pollution, resource depletion, ecosystem services lost). Attempts to measure sustainable economic progress. India's SEEA (System of Environmental-Economic Accounting).

q: Quantitative Easing (QE) involves a central bank:
opts: Raising interest rates to curb inflation
Buying financial assets to inject liquidity
Selling government securities to absorb liquidity
explain: QE: central bank purchases government bonds/other assets from commercial banks to inject money into the economy, lower long-term rates, and stimulate growth when rates near zero.

q: The 'trickle-down effect' in economics has been criticized by economists like:
opts: Joseph Stiglitz, Amartya Sen, and Paul Krugman
explain: IMF's 2015 research (Ostry, Berg, Tsangarides): found that higher income share of top 20% is associated with lower GDP growth; while higher income share of bottom 20% is associated with faster growth. This challenges trickle-down thesis. UNDP, World Bank now emphasize inclusive growth, direct investment in health/education for poor.

q: The Lok Adalat system in India resolves disputes by:
opts: Conciliation and compromise (binding, no court fees)
explain: Lok Adalat (People's Court): alternative dispute resolution forum. Cases are settled by mutual agreement facilitated by a panel (retired judge + lawyers). Benefits: fast (one day), free (no fees), final (no appeal; if no settlement, returns to court). Covers: motor accident claims, labour disputes, matrimonial cases (except divorce), land disputes. Annual disposal: crores of cases.

q: Capital expenditure in the Union Budget includes:
opts: Expenditure that creates assets or reduces liabilities
Current spending on salaries and subsidies (revenue expenditure)
explain: Capital Expenditure (Capex): creates assets or reduces liabilities. Components: Infrastructure (roads, railways, defence equipment), Loans to states and PSUs, Capital infusion in public sector banks, Repayment of public debt. India's Capex in Union Budget: ~Rs 10 lakh crore (2023-24). 'Effective Capex' includes grants-in-aid to states for capex. High capex → productive capacity building.

q: The 'Laffer Curve' in economics shows:
opts: An optimal tax rate that maximizes revenue
Tax revenue always increases with higher tax rate
Tax rates have no effect on economy
explain: Laffer Curve (Arthur Laffer, 1974): at 0% tax rate, revenue = 0; at 100% rate, nobody works, revenue = 0; somewhere in between is the revenue-maximizing rate. Basis for supply-side economics (Reagan's tax cuts). Critics argue the actual peak is above current rates for most countries. Empirical support: mixed.

q: Sen's Capability Approach to development was proposed by:
explain: Amartya Sen (Nobel 1998): capabilities approach — development as freedom/expansion of real opportunities. Focus on what people are actually able to do and be (capabilities), not just income. Influenced HDI design. Major works: 'Development as Freedom' (1999), 'The Idea of Justice'. Bengal famine research: famines caused by lack of entitlements, not just food scarcity.

q: Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana (PMBJP) provides:
opts: Affordable generic medicines via Jan Aushadhi Kendras
explain: PMBJP (Bureau of Pharma PSUs of India — BPPI): network of Jan Aushadhi Kendras selling 1,900+ generic medicines and 300+ surgical items at prices 50-90% below branded alternatives. Ensures quality through testing (ISP and NABL-accredited labs). Benefited: affordable medicines for common diseases (diabetes, hypertension, cardiac, cancer, TB). Also: SuJaK (Sugam Jan Aushadi Kendras) for remote areas.

q: PM CARES Fund (Prime Minister's Citizen Assistance and Relief in Emergency Situations Fund) was established in:
explain: PM CARES Fund was established on March 28, 2020 to deal with COVID-19 pandemic. It is a public charitable trust; donations are tax-exempt under 80G. Separate from PM National Relief Fund.

q: 'Goods and Services Tax Network' (GSTN) is:
explain: GSTN (2013): non-government, non-profit, Section 8 company. Shareholders: Central Govt (20%), State Govts (20% together), financial institutions (HDFC, HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, NSE Strategic Investments, LIC Housing Finance: 60%). Provides IT infrastructure for GST: taxpayer registration, return filing (GSTR-1, GSTR-3B), invoice matching, input tax credit reconciliation, refund processing, analytics.

q: The Feldstein-Horioka Puzzle refers to the high correlation between:
opts: Domestic savings and domestic investment (implying limited capital mobility globally)
explain: Feldstein-Horioka (1980): if capital is globally mobile, domestic savings should flow worldwide seeking highest returns, disconnecting national savings from national investment. But they found high correlation — a 'puzzle.'

q:
With reference to the 'Make in India' initiative, consider the following statements:
1. It was launched in 2014 to promote India as a global manufacturing hub.
2. It seeks to improve the ease of doing business alongside promoting domestic manufacturing.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Both are correct — Make in India was launched in 2014, and improving ease of doing business is an explicit part of the initiative's design.

q: The role of the Finance Commission of India is to:
opts: Recommend how tax revenue is shared between Centre and States
explain: Finance Commission (FC): constitutional body (Article 280), appointed every 5 years by President. 15th FC (NK Singh, 2021-26): recommended 41% of divisible pool to states; performance grants; centrally sponsored scheme reforms. Also recommends grants-in-aid for states. Divisible pool: all central taxes except cess and surcharge.

q: Arthur Lewis's Dual Economy model describes development as movement of labour from:
opts: Traditional agricultural to modern industrial sector
explain: Lewis (1954): unlimited labour supply in subsistence agriculture moves to the industrial/modern sector at a subsistence wage, fueling industrial growth until wages equalize.

q: The Revenue Deficit in the Union Budget is:
opts: Excess of total expenditure over total revenue
explain: Revenue Deficit = Revenue Expenditure - Revenue Receipts. Revenue expenditure: salaries, interest payments, subsidies, defence revenue spending (day-to-day costs, no asset creation). Revenue receipts: tax + non-tax revenues. Fiscal Responsibility: eliminate revenue deficit (target from FRBM). Primary Deficit = Fiscal Deficit minus Interest Payments.

q: The 'multiplier-accelerator interaction' in Keynesian economics explains:
explain: Keynesian business cycle theory: Multiplier (ΔY = k × ΔI) + Accelerator (ΔI = v × ΔY): initial autonomous investment → income multiplied by k → higher income accelerates further investment → boom (expansion). When income growth slows, acceleration reverses, investment falls, income multiplier works downward → recession. Paul Samuelson formalized this interaction.

q:
With reference to informal sector employment in India, consider the following statements:
1. A large share of India's workforce is employed in the informal/unorganised sector.
2. Informal sector workers typically lack access to formal social security benefits.
3. Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) is used to track employment/unemployment data in India.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
explain: All three are correct and standard, well-documented facts about India's labour market structure. Hence 1, 2 and 3.

q: Direct taxes are taxes paid directly by:
opts: The person/entity on whom it is levied (cannot be shifted) — Income Tax, Corporate Tax, Capital Gains Tax, Wealth Tax (abolished 2016)
Consumer who passes it on (indirect taxes like GST, customs)
explain: Direct Taxes: levied on and collected from the same person (incidence and impact on same entity). Income Tax (individuals), Corporate Tax, Capital Gains Tax, Securities Transaction Tax. Administered by CBDT (Central Board of Direct Taxes). Indirect Taxes: GST, customs duty — taxpayer passes burden to consumer. Administered by CBIC.

q: The term 'poverty line' in India is determined by:
opts: Minimum per capita expenditure for basic needs (Tendulkar/Rangarajan methodology)
explain: India's Poverty Line: Tendulkar Committee (2009): Rs 816/month urban, Rs 672/month rural (2011-12 prices). Rangarajan Committee (2014): higher threshold — Rs 1407 urban, Rs 972 rural. SECC (Socio-Economic and Caste Census) used for targeting welfare programs. About 21% of population below poverty line (World Bank $1.90/day PPP criterion).

q: The Bharat Broadband Network Limited (BBNL) was merged with BSNL to implement:
explain: BBNL (Bharat Broadband Network Limited, 2012): Special Purpose Vehicle to implement BharatNet (initially NOFN). In 2023, government merged BBNL with BSNL to streamline the BharatNet project and leverage BSNL's existing infrastructure, workforce, and right-of-way permissions for faster rural broadband rollout.

q:
Consider the following statements about India's foreign exchange reserves:
1. Foreign exchange reserves include foreign currency assets, gold, SDRs and India's reserve position with the IMF.
2. The Reserve Bank of India manages India's foreign exchange reserves.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Both are correct — the composition of forex reserves and RBI's role in managing them are accurate facts.

q: The 'Gross Value Added' (GVA) concept in India's national accounts means:
explain: GVA = GDP at basic prices = value of output (production) minus value of intermediate consumption (inputs used). GDP at market prices = GVA + Net Taxes on Products (taxes - subsidies on products). India's 2011-12 base year revision introduced GVA-based reporting. GVA by sector: Agriculture, Industry (manufacturing, mining, utilities, construction), Services.

q: The Tamil Nadu Industrial Development Corporation (TIDCO) was established to:
opts: Promote and facilitate industrial development in Tamil Nadu
explain: TIDCO (1965): TN's state government industrial promotion company. Functions: promotes investment, sets up joint ventures with private companies, participates in equity of industrial projects, and develops sector-specific parks. Examples of TIDCO JVs: TANCEM (cement), TANTRANSCO (power), TIDEL Park (IT park in Chennai).

q: The Capital to Risk-weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) under Basel III norms requires banks to maintain minimum:
explain: Basel III: minimum CRAR = 8% + Capital Conservation Buffer 2.5% = 10.5% total. India's RBI requires 9% minimum. CRAR = Total Capital / Risk-Weighted Assets.

q: The term 'fiscal deficit' refers to:
opts: Excess of total government expenditure over total revenue receipts (tax + non-tax revenue) — financed by borrowing
Excess of exports over imports (trade surplus)
Excess of imports over exports (trade deficit)
Excess of bank deposits over loans
explain: Fiscal Deficit = Total Expenditure - (Revenue Receipts + Capital Receipts excluding borrowings). It shows government's borrowing requirement. India's fiscal deficit target: 3% of GDP (FRBM Act, 2003 target). Funded by borrowing from RBI (monetization, inflationary) or market borrowings (public debt). High fiscal deficit → high government debt.

q: NABARD stands for:
opts: National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development
National Banking Authority for Regional Development
National Association for Banking and Rural Districts
explain: NABARD (National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development) was established in 1982. It provides credit for agricultural and rural development and supervises cooperative banks and RRBs.

q:
Consider the following statements regarding the FRBM Act, 2003:
1. It aims to ensure fiscal discipline by setting targets for fiscal and revenue deficits.
2. It mandates the government to lay a Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement before Parliament.
3. It has never been amended since its enactment in 2003.
4. It allows for deviation from fiscal targets in situations like national security threats or calamities.
How many of the above statements are correct?
explain: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. Statement 3 is incorrect — the FRBM Act has been amended multiple times (e.g., 2004, 2012, 2018) to revise targets and timelines. Hence only three.

q: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) 2016 was enacted to:
opts: Provide time-bound resolution of insolvency/bankruptcy cases
explain: IBC 2016: unified framework for resolving insolvency. Process: creditor/debtor files, Resolution Professional appointed, Committee of Creditors evaluates resolution plans within 180+90 days. Failing resolution → liquidation. Improved India's ranking in World Bank's Ease of Doing Business: Resolving Insolvency indicator improved dramatically.

q: The 'Phillips Curve' shows the relationship between:
opts: Unemployment rate and inflation rate (inverse relationship)
explain: A.W. Phillips (1958) found an inverse relationship between unemployment and inflation. Low unemployment → higher wages → higher spending → higher inflation. This relationship broke down in 1970s stagflation.

q: The Second Five Year Plan (1956-61) was based on the model by:
explain: Second FYP (Mahalanobis Plan, 1956-61): focused on heavy industry and capital goods (Feldman-Mahalanobis model — investment in capital goods to boost long-term growth). Steel plants: Bhilai (Soviet assistance), Durgapur (British), Rourkela (West German). Also established IITs and other institutions.

q: India's Foreign Trade Policy 2023-28 sets a target for merchandise and services exports by 2030 of:
explain: FTP 2023-28 (effective April 1, 2023): target $2 trillion merchandise + $1 trillion services exports by 2030 = $3 trillion total. Key focus: e-commerce exports, ease of doing business, districts as export hubs.

q: Monopsony refers to a market where there is:
explain: Monopsony = single buyer with market power over sellers (opposite of monopoly). E.g., single employer in a company town (wage setting below competitive level). Labour market monopsonies are common.

q: Which of the following is a direct tax?
explain: Direct taxes are paid directly to the government by the person on whom they are levied (e.g., Income Tax, Corporate Tax, Wealth Tax). Indirect taxes (GST, Customs, Excise) are collected through an intermediary.

q:
With reference to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016, consider the following statements:
1. It provides a time-bound process for resolving insolvency of companies and individuals.
2. The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) is the adjudicating authority for corporate insolvency under the IBC.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Both are correct — the IBC's time-bound resolution process and the NCLT's role as adjudicating authority for corporate insolvency are accurate.

q: India's 'National Mission on Transformative Mobility and Battery Storage' (NMTMBS) aims at:
explain: EV Mission: FAME India (Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of Electric Vehicles): Phase-I (2015-19), Phase-II (2019-24, Rs 10,000 crore): subsidies for EV purchase, charging infrastructure. PLI for Advanced Chemistry Cell batteries (ACC-PLI, Rs 18,100 crore). NMTMBS: inter-ministerial mission for EV ecosystem. India wants 30% EV by 2030 for all categories; 100% EV for 2-wheelers and 3-wheelers.

q: The Asian Development Bank (ADB) is headquartered in:
explain: ADB (Asian Development Bank, 1966): HQ in Manila, Philippines. 68 member countries (49 from Asia-Pacific). Provides: project loans, policy-based loans, technical assistance, equity investments. India is one of ADB's largest borrowers (infrastructure, urban development, agriculture). USA and Japan are largest shareholders.

q: The Harrod-Domar model of economic growth emphasizes the role of:
explain: Harrod-Domar: Growth Rate = Savings Rate / Capital-Output Ratio. Higher savings → higher investment → higher growth. Used to justify foreign aid (filling 'savings gap') for developing countries.

q: The Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) was launched on:
explain: PMJDY launched August 28, 2014 — National Mission for Financial Inclusion. Features: zero-balance account, RuPay debit card, Rs 1 lakh accident insurance, Rs 30,000 life cover, overdraft facility. Guinness record for most accounts opened in a week.

q: The concept of 'Financial Repression' refers to:
opts: High interest rates imposed by central banks
Interest rates kept below inflation, taxing savers to benefit borrowers
Restrictions on foreign banks operating in India
Reducing credit to the private sector
explain: Financial Repression: government caps interest rates below inflation rate, making real rates negative. Savers lose; government borrows cheaply (financial sector 'repressed'). Common in post-WWII period and some developing nations.

q: India's 'Ease of Living' index measures:
opts: Quality of life in Indian cities
Same as Ease of Doing Business
explain: Ease of Living Index (Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, 2018, updated 2020): assesses quality of life in Indian cities (111 cities). Four pillars: Governance (20%), Social (30%), Economic (20%), Physical (30%). Assessed at: services (58%) and outcomes (42%). Also: Municipal Performance Index (MPI) for city governance. Bengaluru, Pune, Ahmedabad, Chennai have topped rankings.

q: India's Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 classified industries into schedules. Schedule A industries were exclusively reserved for:
explain: IPR 1956: Schedule A (17 industries) — exclusive State domain (arms, atomic energy, railways, coal, steel). Schedule B — State to establish, private allowed. Schedule C — private sector.

q: Food Corporation of India (FCI) was established to:
opts: Procure food grains at MSP and distribute via PDS
explain: FCI (1965, FCI Act 1964): functions: procurement of wheat and rice from farmers at MSP (mainly Punjab, Haryana, UP), building and managing strategic food reserves (buffer stocks), distributing to state governments for PDS at Central Issue Price (CIP). FCI's buffer stock of grain helps stabilize prices and ensure food security.

q: India's UPI (Unified Payments Interface) was developed by:
explain: UPI: developed by NPCI (National Payments Corporation of India) in 2016, launched April 11, 2016. Enables instant 24×7 inter-bank fund transfers via mobile. India processes ~10 billion UPI transactions/month (2023).

q: The National Health Mission (NHM) ASHA workers are:
explain: ASHA (Accredited Social Health Activist): female community health worker (Class 8 educated, 25+ years, married/widowed/divorced). Functions: promote institutional deliveries, immunization, family planning, TB treatment adherence; accompany patients to health facilities; receive performance-based incentives. About 10 lakh ASHAs in India.

q: The concept of 'creative destruction' in economics was given by:
explain: Creative Destruction (Schumpeter): capitalism's engine of growth is innovation. New technologies, products, and firms continuously destroy old ones — enabling higher productivity and better products. Example: automobiles destroyed horse carriages, internet destroyed physical retail (Amazon vs Sears), smartphones destroyed camera and music player industries. Short-term disruption, long-term growth.

q: India's Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) was set up to:
opts: Regulate insolvency professionals and agencies under IBC 2016
explain: IBBI (2016): statutory body under IBC 2016. Functions: regulate insolvency professionals (IPs who manage resolution), insolvency professional agencies, information utilities (NeSL — National e-Governance Services Ltd). Also lays down regulations for conducting CIRP (Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process) and Liquidation processes.

q: The concept of 'Social Banking' was introduced in India after:
explain: Social Banking: using banks as instruments of social development, not just profit-making. After 1969 nationalization: banks were directed to open branches in unbanked areas, meet PSL targets, provide small loans, implement government welfare schemes. Lead Bank Scheme (1970): one bank assigned leadership role in each district for financial inclusion.

q: The 'SDG India Index' is published by:
explain: SDG India Index (NITI Aayog, first edition 2018-19): quantifies state/UT progress on SDGs. States ranked: Frontrunner (65-100), Performer (50-64), Aspirant (0-49). Indicators cover: no poverty, zero hunger, good health, quality education, gender equality, clean water, energy, economic growth, reduced inequality, sustainable cities, climate action, etc. Kerala, Himachal Pradesh, Tamil Nadu consistently top performers.

q: The concept of 'Invisible Hand' introduced by Adam Smith suggests that:
opts: Individual self-interest in free markets leads to efficient resource allocation for society
explain: Adam Smith's 'Invisible Hand' (Wealth of Nations, 1776): individuals pursuing their own interest in free markets unintentionally promote society's economic well-being. Foundation of laissez-faire capitalism.

q: The 'Laffer Curve' illustrates the relationship between:
opts: Tax rate and tax revenue — showing that revenue peaks at an optimal tax rate
Money supply and interest rates (LM Curve)
explain: The Laffer Curve shows that both 0% and 100% tax rates result in zero revenue. Tax revenue peaks at some optimal rate. It is used to argue for tax cuts to increase revenue.

q: A Veblen good is characterized by:
opts: Demand increasing as price rises due to conspicuous consumption
explain: Veblen goods (Thorstein Veblen): luxury goods where higher price signals higher status, increasing demand (diamonds, luxury cars, designer goods). Upward-sloping demand curve.

q: The term 'repo' stands for:
explain: Repo (Repurchase Agreement): one party sells securities (government bonds) to another and agrees to repurchase them at a later date at a specified (higher) price. The difference represents the interest (repo rate). In RBI context: commercial banks sell G-Secs to RBI for overnight liquidity, agreeing to repurchase next day. Reverse Repo: opposite direction — banks buy from RBI.

q: The AMRUT (Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation) scheme focuses on:
opts: Basic urban infrastructure (water, sewerage, parks) for cities
explain: AMRUT (2015, replaced JNNURM): provides every household with a tap with assured supply of water and a sewerage connection; parks and public spaces. 500 cities. AMRUT 2.0 (2021-26): 100% coverage of urban water supply, 100% sewerage management, rejuvenation of water bodies, and operational & maintenance reforms.

q: Which money supply measure in India includes Currency with Public + Demand Deposits + Other Deposits with RBI?
explain: M1 = Currency with public + Demand deposits with banks + Other deposits with RBI. M0 = Reserve Money (monetary base). M3 = Broad Money (M1 + time deposits).

q: What is the role of the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) of India in public finance?
opts: Audit all government expenditure and receipts
explain: CAG (Article 148): supreme audit institution. Audits accounts of Union and State governments, PSUs. Reports tabled in Parliament (Union) and State Legislatures. Independent of executive; reports to President.

q: The term 'Stagflation' was coined during which decade and event?
explain: Stagflation = stagnation + inflation. Coined by UK politician Iain Macleod in 1965, but the phenomenon prominently occurred in the 1970s OPEC oil crises (1973, 1979). Contradicted the Phillips Curve.

q: The Fifteenth Finance Commission (15th FC) recommended which tax devolution share to states?
explain: 15th Finance Commission (NK Singh, 2021-26): recommended 41% of divisible pool to states (1% less than 14th FC's 42%). Reason: J&K became 2 UTs — the 1% that was going to J&K state now goes to central government for UTs. Grants: Rs 10.3 lakh crore to states. Performance-based grants for health, education, urban bodies, PRIs.

q: Price elasticity of demand (PED) measures:
opts: % change in quantity demanded / % change in price
explain: PED = %ΔQd / %ΔP. Elastic (|PED|>1): consumer responds strongly to price changes — luxury goods (gold jewelry, cars). Inelastic (|PED|<1): quantity barely changes with price — necessities (salt, insulin, petrol). Unit elastic (|PED|=1): %ΔQd = %ΔP. Key for tax policy: taxing inelastic goods (petrol, tobacco) raises more revenue with less market distortion.

q: Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) is:
explain: FDI: foreign entity invests in a domestic company (typically 10%+ equity = significant control). Brings: capital, technology, management expertise, global market access. FPI/FII: foreign portfolio investment (buying shares without control). India attracted $70 billion+ FDI in 2021-22. Top FDI sectors: services, computer, telecom, construction.

q: The 'Marginal Standing Facility' (MSF) rate is:
opts: Overnight borrowing rate from RBI against G-Secs (ceiling rate)
explain: MSF (Marginal Standing Facility): banks borrow overnight from RBI pledging G-Secs (even those earmarked for SLR) up to 2% of NDTL. MSF rate = Repo Rate + 25 bps (upper bound of LAF corridor). It provides a safety valve for banks in extreme liquidity crunch. SDF (Standing Deposit Facility) is the floor = Repo Rate - 25 bps.
