explain: Negative Income Tax (Friedman, 'Capitalism and Freedom,' 1962): replace complex welfare bureaucracy with a simple system — at incomes below a threshold, government pays subsidies; above threshold, people pay taxes. Set the threshold and rate carefully. More efficient than targeted programs. Inspired UBI concepts. US pilot experiments in 1970s showed some reduction in work effort.

q: Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY (Jan Arogya Yojana) provides health cover of how much per family per year?
explain: PM-JAY (launched September 23, 2018): Rs 5 lakh per family per year for secondary and tertiary care hospitalization. World's largest government health insurance scheme. ~55 crore beneficiaries (50 crore poor).

q: The credit multiplier (money multiplier) is the reciprocal of:
explain: Credit Multiplier = 1/CRR. If CRR = 4%, multiplier = 25. Every Rs 1 of base money creates Rs 25 of deposits. Higher CRR → lower multiplier → less credit creation.

q: India's 'Digital Rupee' (Central Bank Digital Currency — CBDC) was launched as a pilot by:
explain: e-Rupee (CBDC): RBI launched pilots: Wholesale CBDC (e₹-W, November 1, 2022): for settlement of secondary market transactions in government securities among selected banks. Retail CBDC (e₹-R, December 1, 2022): for use by general public — like digital cash, interoperable, no bank account needed, distributed by selected banks. Eventually to replace/supplement physical cash.

q: The Union Budget is presented by the:
explain: The Finance Minister presents the Union Budget to Parliament (Lok Sabha) on 1 February every year (changed from last day of February in 2017). It outlines government revenue and expenditure for the coming year.

q: India's Logistics Performance Index (LPI) rank has been improving. The LPI is published by the:
explain: Logistics Performance Index: World Bank biennial survey. Ranks countries on customs efficiency, infrastructure, international shipments, logistics competence, tracking, timeliness. India ranked 38 in 2023.

q: The 'Mundell-Fleming Model' extends Keynesian IS-LM analysis to:
opts: Open economies with capital flows and exchange rates
explain: The Mundell-Fleming model (early 1960s) extends IS-LM to open economies, incorporating international capital flows and exchange rate policies. It shows that monetary and fiscal policy effectiveness depends on the exchange rate regime.

q: The Integrated Ombudsman Scheme of RBI (2021) covers complaints against:
opts: All RBI-regulated entities (banks, NBFCs, PPI issuers)
explain: RB-IOS 2021 (Reserve Bank — Integrated Ombudsman Scheme): unified, one-nation-one-ombudsman platform. Covers: all SCBs (public, private, foreign), RRBs, Small Finance Banks, NBFCs with assets > Rs 100 crore, Non-bank PPI issuers (Paytm, PhonePe). No geographical limitation — complaint filed online centrally. Replaces 3 separate ombudsman schemes.

q: Nash Equilibrium (game theory) is a situation where:
opts: Both players cooperate to maximize joint outcome
No player can benefit by changing strategy given the other player's strategy
The government intervenes to set prices
explain: Nash Equilibrium (John Nash, Nobel 1994): each player's strategy is the best response to others' strategies — no one has incentive to deviate. Prisoner's Dilemma is the classic example.

q: The concept of 'Demographic Dividend' for India refers to the economic benefit arising from:
opts: Large elderly population needing care industry
Large working-age population relative to dependents (young + old)
explain: Demographic Dividend: large working-age population (15-64) relative to dependents boosts savings, investment, and growth. India's window: ~2020-2040. Median age ~28 years. Requires jobs and skill development.

q: The 'Tobin Tax' is proposed for:
opts: Small tax on international financial transactions to reduce speculation
explain: The Tobin Tax (proposed by James Tobin, 1972) is a small tax on international currency transactions to reduce speculative short-term financial flows ('hot money') without impeding long-term investment.

q: Which method of calculating GDP sums up wages, profits, rent, and interest paid in the economy?
explain: Income Method: GDP = Compensation of Employees + Gross Operating Surplus + Gross Mixed Income + Taxes − Subsidies on production. Sums factor incomes generated in production.

q: The Consolidated Fund of India is governed by which Article of the Constitution?
explain: Article 266 establishes the Consolidated Fund of India. All revenues, loans raised, and loan repayments received by the Government of India go into this fund.

q: The law of demand states that, all else equal:
opts: Price rises, quantity demanded falls (inverse relationship)
explain: Law of Demand (Alfred Marshall): price and quantity demanded have an inverse relationship — as price rises, quantity demanded falls (consumers buy less; some switch to substitutes). Exceptions (Giffen goods, Veblen goods, necessities, wartime hoarding). Demand curve slopes downward.

q: IRDAI (Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India) was established to:
opts: Regulate and develop the insurance industry
explain: IRDAI (1999, under IRDA Act 1999): insurance sector regulator. Regulates: LIC (Life Insurance Corporation), private life insurance companies, general insurance (motor, health, fire, marine), and reinsurance (GIC Re). Insurance sector opened to private players in 2000. FDI in insurance: increased to 74% in 2021. HQ: Hyderabad.

q: Tamil Nadu's SIPCOT (State Industries Promotion Corporation of Tamil Nadu) primarily promotes:
opts: Medium and large industries by developing industrial parks and SEZs
explain: SIPCOT (1971): develops industrial parks, estates, and SEZs for medium/large industries in Tamil Nadu. Has 60+ industrial parks. SIDCO (1970) handles small industries.

q: The Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme provides incentive as a percentage of:
opts: Incremental sales over a base year
explain: PLI: companies receive incentive (4-20% depending on sector) on incremental sales above their base year (2019-20). Covers 14 sectors. Aims to attract investment, enhance manufacturing, and boost exports.

q: Masala Bonds are rupee-denominated bonds issued by Indian entities in:
opts: Only in the London Stock Exchange
explain: Masala Bonds: rupee-denominated bonds issued by Indian entities (corporates, government-backed) in overseas markets. Currency risk borne by foreign investors. First issued by IFC (World Bank arm) in 2014 on LSE.

q: The PM Gati Shakti National Master Plan was launched in:
explain: PM Gati Shakti (October 2021): national master plan to bring about integrated, seamless, multi-modal connectivity. Digital platform integrating 16 ministries: Roads, Railways, Waterways, Aviation, Ports, Mass Transport, Logistics, Power, Pipelines, Telecom. Eliminates siloed planning; identifies bottlenecks. Aim: reduce logistics costs (currently ~14% of GDP vs global benchmark ~8%).

q: The 'Bharat Stage' emission standards for vehicles (BS-VI since 2020) are India's equivalent of:
explain: Bharat Stage (BS) emission standards: based on European emission norms. India leapfrogged BS-V and went directly from BS-IV to BS-VI (April 1, 2020 — ahead of many countries). BS-VI equivalent to Euro-VI: drastic reduction in particulate matter (PM) and oxides of nitrogen (NOx). Required oil companies to supply BS-VI fuel, vehicle manufacturers to retrofit engines.

q: India's tax administration reforms include:
opts: Faceless Assessment, Taxpayer Charter, DIN, pre-filled ITR, Vivad se Vishwas
explain: Income Tax reforms under 'Transparent Taxation — Honouring the Honest' (2020): Faceless Assessment (all appeals and assessments done online, randomly allocated, no geographic/taxpayer-officer nexus), Taxpayer Charter (rights and responsibilities defined), DIN on every tax notice/letter (verifiable online), pre-filled ITR forms, Vivad se Vishwas (2020, settling 4.8 lakh tax disputes of Rs 9.32 lakh crore).

q: The concept of 'crowdfunding' as a source of startup finance means:
opts: Raising small sums from many people online
explain: Crowdfunding: raising capital from many small contributors online. Types: Reward-based (backers get product/service — Kickstarter, Indiegogo), Equity-based (backers get shares — regulated by SEBI in India as 'crowd sourcing/alternative investment'), Debt-based (peer-to-peer lending), Donation-based (charity). SEBI issued framework for Social Stock Exchanges (2022) for nonprofit crowdfunding.

q:
Consider the following statements on agricultural marketing reforms:
1. APMC (Agricultural Produce Market Committee) Acts historically required farmers to sell produce only through regulated mandis.
2. e-NAM (National Agriculture Market) is an electronic trading platform aiming to integrate agricultural markets across states.
3. Contract farming involves an agreement between farmers and buyers fixed before the growing season.
4. Agricultural marketing in India has always been completely free of any government regulation.
How many of the above statements are correct?
explain: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is incorrect and directly contradicts Statement 1 — APMC Acts represent significant historical government regulation of agricultural marketing. Hence only three.

q:
Consider the following statements about India's banking structure:
1. Scheduled Commercial Banks include Public Sector Banks, Private Sector Banks, Foreign Banks and Regional Rural Banks.
2. Payments Banks in India are permitted to accept demand deposits but cannot issue loans or credit cards directly.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Both are correct — the classification of scheduled commercial banks and the restricted (deposit-only, no-lending) mandate of Payments Banks are accurate as per RBI's licensing framework.

q: Index of Industrial Production (IIP) measures:
opts: Monthly change in industrial output volume
explain: IIP (Index of Industrial Production): compiled by National Statistical Office (NSO). Measures changes in industrial output (mining: ~14%, manufacturing: ~78%, electricity: ~8% by weight). Base year: 2011-12. Released monthly (with 6-week lag). Key indicator for industrial health and monetary policy decisions.

q: Open Acreage Licensing Policy (OALP) in India is related to:
explain: HELP (Hydrocarbon Exploration and Licensing Policy, 2016) replaced NELP (New Exploration and Licensing Policy). Features: revenue sharing model (replaces production sharing contracts), uniform licensing (oil, gas, CBM, shale in one licence), OALP (Open Acreage Licensing — companies choose any available block from data repository). Aims to boost domestic oil/gas production.

q: Credit Default Swaps (CDS) are financial instruments that:
opts: Transfer credit risk from buyer to seller for a premium
Are a type of government bond
Are used only for currency trading
explain: CDS (Credit Default Swap): a derivative that works like insurance on a bond. If the reference entity (company/country) defaults, the CDS seller pays the buyer the face value. AIG's massive CDS exposure caused its near-collapse in 2008 (US government bailout: $182 billion). Warren Buffett called derivatives 'weapons of mass financial destruction.'

q: India's base year for National Income calculation was revised in 2015 from 2004-05 to:
explain: In January 2015, CSO (now NSO) revised the base year for GDP calculation to 2011-12 from 2004-05. Also shifted to GDP at market prices from GDP at factor cost as primary aggregate.

q: The National Infrastructure and Investment Fund (NIIF) is different from NIP because:
opts: NIIF is an investing fund; NIP is a project pipeline/plan
NIIF is private, NIP is public
explain: NIIF (National Infrastructure and Investment Fund, 2015): an institution — invests in infrastructure through three funds (Master, Fund of Funds, Strategic Opportunities). Sovereign wealth fund characteristics with 49% govt ownership. NIP (National Infrastructure Pipeline, 2019): a planning document listing 6,835+ infrastructure projects worth Rs 111 lakh crore for 2019-25. Two distinct instruments.

q: India's GDP composition (2022-23 estimates) shows which sector contributing the most to GDP?
explain: India's GDP by sector (2022-23): Services ~55%, Industry ~25-28%, Agriculture ~17-18%. Services (IT, finance, trade, transport) dominate GDP. But agriculture employs ~45% of workforce — structural dualism.

q: According to Keynes, during recession the government should:
opts: Increase government spending and reduce taxes (expansionary fiscal policy)
explain: Keynesian economics recommends expansionary fiscal policy during recession — increase government spending (even deficit spending) and reduce taxes to stimulate aggregate demand and employment.

q: Which government body is primarily responsible for compiling and releasing India's national income (GDP) estimates?
explain: The National Statistical Office (NSO), under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI), compiles and releases India's official GDP/national income estimates.

q: Demonetization in India (November 8, 2016) scrapped currency notes of which denominations?
explain: Demonetization (November 8, 2016): PM Modi announced scrapping of Rs 500 and Rs 1000 notes (86% of currency in circulation). New Rs 500 and Rs 2000 notes introduced. Aims: counter black money, counterfeit, terror financing.

q: The Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) under IBC 2016 must be completed in:
explain: CIRP (Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process) under IBC: 180 days from admission. Can extend by 90 days (NCLT approval). If no resolution plan approved within 270 days (330 with litigation-excluded period) → liquidation. NCLT (National Company Law Tribunal) adjudicates IBC cases. Success stories: Essar Steel, Bhushan Steel resolved through IBC (ArcelorMittal, Tata Steel as acquirers).

q: The Atal Pension Yojana (APY) targets:
explain: APY (2015, replaced Swavalamban scheme): for unorganized sector workers. Subscribers aged 18-40 contribute monthly; at 60, receive guaranteed pension of Rs 1,000/2,000/3,000/4,000/5,000 per month. Government (co-contribution of 50% of contribution or Rs 1,000/year, whichever lower) for eligible subscribers for 5 years. Administered by PFRDA (Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority).

q: Crowdfunding is regulated in India by:
explain: SEBI regulates equity/securities-based crowdfunding. RBI regulates peer-to-peer (P2P) lending (a form of crowdfunding) through NBFC-P2P guidelines (2017). Donation/reward crowdfunding largely unregulated.

q: Tamil Nadu's 'Vision Tamil Nadu 2023' document set a target of making Tamil Nadu:
explain: Tamil Nadu Vision 2023: target to become a $1 trillion economy. TN is among India's top 3 economies (after Maharashtra and UP in GDP terms, or top 2-3 depending on year). GDP ~Rs 27 lakh crore (2023-24).

q: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) 2016 established the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) as the:
opts: Adjudicating authority for corporate insolvency resolution
explain: IBC 2016: NCLT is the adjudicating authority for corporate insolvency (companies). NCLT approves resolution plan. DRT (Debt Recovery Tribunal) handles individual/partnership insolvency. IBBI is the regulator.

q: The 'Lead Bank Scheme' in India was launched to:
opts: Assign one bank as 'lead bank' for each district
Make one bank responsible for all banking in a district
explain: Lead Bank Scheme (1969): one bank (public sector) designated as lead bank per district (covering all talukas). Functions: preparing annual credit plan (ACP) for the district, coordinating with other banks, promoting financial inclusion, leading SLBC (State Level Bankers' Committee) work in the district. Essential for priority sector credit planning and rural financial inclusion.

q: India's 'Silent Revolution' in agriculture refers to:
opts: Second Green Revolution for eastern India
explain: Second Green Revolution/Evergreen Revolution (M.S. Swaminathan): need to extend agricultural productivity gains to eastern India and dryland farming regions while maintaining ecological sustainability. Also: shift from cereal monoculture to diversification (horticulture, dairying, poultry, fisheries) for nutritional security and farmer income.

q: The Green Revolution (1960s-70s) was associated with:
explain: Green Revolution: Norman Borlaug (USA, Nobel 1970) developed semi-dwarf wheat varieties (higher yield, resistant to lodging — bending with wind). Introduced to India by M.S. Swaminathan (who worked with IARI) under Agriculture Minister C. Subramaniam and PM Indira Gandhi's government. Punjab/Haryana became wheat-surplus states. Pakistan, Mexico also benefited. Also: IR-8 'miracle rice' (IRRI, Philippines).

q: India's 'One Nation One Ration Card' (ONORC) scheme allows:
opts: Claiming PDS entitlement from any Fair Price Shop in India
explain: ONORC (2019-2021, nationwide rollout): using Aadhaar-linked biometric authentication at FPS (Fair Price Shop), beneficiary can claim PDS quota from any FPS in India. Critical for: migrant workers (can claim entitlement at destination state), seasonal migrants. All 36 states/UTs joined ONORC by 2021. 80+ crore beneficiaries. Managed through Integrated Management of PDS (IM-PDS) portal.

q: Tirupur city in Tamil Nadu is known as:
explain: Tirupur (Tiruppur): world's largest exporter of knitted cotton garments. About 6,000 garment units, ~600,000 workers. Export markets: UK, USA, EU, Australia. Exports ~$4 billion annually. 'Dollar City' because of high foreign exchange earnings. Also known as 'Banian City' for banian/vest production.

q: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) was established in:
explain: RBI: established April 1, 1935, as a private shareholders' bank under the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 (based on Hilton-Young Commission recommendations). Nationalized January 1, 1949. Governor: Shaktikanta Das (26th Governor). HQ: Mumbai. Key functions: monetary policy, currency issue, banking regulation, forex management.

q: The Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) is a scheme for:
explain: PMFBY (February 2016): replaced NAIS and MNAIS. Features: uniform premium of 2% for kharif crops, 1.5% for rabi crops, 5% for commercial/horticultural crops; remaining premium paid by Centre and State equally. Uses satellite, remote sensing, and smartphone apps for rapid loss assessment. Covers pre-sowing to post-harvest losses.

q: The Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) launched in 2016 replaced which earlier crop insurance schemes?
opts: NAIS (National Agricultural Insurance Scheme) and MNAIS
explain: PMFBY (January 2016): replaced NAIS (1999) and MNAIS (2010). Premium rates: Kharif 2%, Rabi 1.5%, commercial/horticultural crops 5%. Actuarial premium difference borne by Centre and State.

q:
With reference to food security in India, consider the following statements:
1. The National Food Security Act, 2013 provides a legal entitlement to subsidised foodgrains for a specified proportion of the population.
2. The Public Distribution System (PDS) is the main mechanism for distributing subsidised foodgrains.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Both are correct — the NFSA 2013 provides legal food entitlements, and the PDS is the main distribution mechanism for it.

q: The 'trickle-down' theory of economic growth argues:
opts: Growth benefits top sectors that eventually trickle down to the poor
Only the poor should be targeted
explain: Trickle-down economics (supply-side economics): tax cuts and benefits to rich/corporations will create investment, jobs, and economic activity that benefits all. Critics (e.g., Amartya Sen, Joseph Stiglitz): growth doesn't automatically reduce inequality; direct investment in human capital (health, education) is more effective for inclusive growth.

q: Priority Sector Lending (PSL) norms require banks to lend:
explain: PSL: RBI mandates Scheduled Commercial Banks lend 40% of ANBC to priority sectors. Subsectors: Agriculture (18% of ANBC, of which 8% for small/marginal farmers), MSMEs, Education, Housing (affordable), Renewable Energy, Social Infrastructure. Foreign banks with <20 branches: 40% (different sub-targets). Priority Sector Lending Certificates (PSLCs) allow trading PSL shortfalls/surplus among banks.

q: The National Investment and Infrastructure Fund (NIIF) was set up to:
explain: NIIF (2015): India's quasi-sovereign wealth fund for infrastructure. 49% owned by Government of India; 51% by foreign/domestic institutional investors (Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, Singapore GIC, etc.). Three funds: Master Fund (greenfield/brownfield infra), Fund of Funds, Strategic Opportunities Fund. Total committed capital: ~$4.5 billion.

q: The term 'Laissez-Faire' in economics means:
explain: Laissez-faire (French: 'let do/let go'): economic philosophy advocating minimal government intervention. Markets, through price mechanism ('invisible hand' — Adam Smith, 'Wealth of Nations,' 1776), efficiently allocate resources. Associated with classical economics. Opposite: interventionism/planned economy.

q: Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) theory suggests that exchange rates should equalize:
explain: PPP: exchange rates adjust so that identical goods cost the same across countries. The 'Big Mac Index' by The Economist is a popular PPP measure.

q: The concept of 'micro, small, and medium enterprises' (MSMEs) in India is defined based on:
opts: Investment in plant & machinery and annual turnover
explain: Revised MSME definition (May 2020): Micro: investment ≤Rs 1 crore AND turnover ≤Rs 5 crore. Small: investment ≤Rs 10 crore AND turnover ≤Rs 50 crore. Medium: investment ≤Rs 50 crore AND turnover ≤Rs 250 crore. MSMEs: ~63 million units, 30% of GDP, 45% of exports, 110+ million employed.

q: 'Cooperative federalism' in India refers to:
opts: Centre and States working together collaboratively
explain: Cooperative Federalism: Centre-State partnership and cooperation. Examples: GST Council (Centre+States jointly decide tax rates), Finance Commission (balances Centre-State fiscal needs), NITI Aayog (PM+CMs meet as Governing Council), CSS (Centrally Sponsored Schemes: Centre+State funding). Competitive federalism: states competing for investment ('ease of doing business' rankings).

q:
With reference to India's foreign trade policy, consider the following statements:
1. The Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) formulates and implements India's Foreign Trade Policy.
2. Special Economic Zones (SEZs) are treated as foreign territory for the purposes of trade operations and duties.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Both are correct — DGFT administers the Foreign Trade Policy, and SEZs are treated as foreign territory for trade/tariff purposes.

q: Which Five Year Plan was the most successful in India in terms of achieving its growth target?
explain: Sixth FYP (1980-85): India's most successful plan — exceeded its growth target. Focus: poverty alleviation, self-reliance, minimum needs program. Also notable: Third FYP (1961-66) was derailed by 1962 India-China war, 1965 India-Pakistan war, and drought → 'plan holiday' 1966-69. Eleventh FYP (2007-12) achieved 7.9% growth.

q: The Revenue Deficit is defined as:
explain: Revenue Deficit = Revenue Expenditure − Revenue Receipts. Shows that current (non-capital) spending exceeds current income, meaning government borrows even for day-to-day expenses (not just investment). Negative for fiscal health.

q: The Kuznets Curve (Environmental Kuznets Curve) suggests:
opts: Pollution rises then falls as income rises (inverted U)
Income inequality always rises with growth
explain: Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC): as income rises, pollution/environmental degradation first increases (industrialization), reaches a peak, then decreases (clean technology, service economy, environmental regulations). Named after Simon Kuznets. The original Kuznets Curve deals with income inequality (inverted U) as economic development progresses.

q: Which scheme is popularly referred to by the acronym MGNREGA and provides a legal guarantee of rural employment?
opts: Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act
explain: MGNREGA is the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, providing a legal right to rural employment.

q: The concept of 'Comparative Advantage' in international trade was developed by:
explain: Comparative Advantage (Ricardo): a country should specialize in goods where it has the lowest opportunity cost relative to other goods, not necessarily the lowest absolute cost. Even if one country is more efficient in all goods, both benefit from trade through specialization. Basis for international free trade theory. Example: India in IT services, China in manufacturing.

q: The term 'quantitative easing' (QE) refers to:
opts: Central bank buys assets to inject money into the economy
explain: QE: when conventional monetary policy (lowering interest rates) is insufficient (near-zero rates), central bank creates money and buys assets (government bonds, MBS) from banks. This: increases banks' reserves, lowers long-term interest rates, boosts credit, and stimulates economy. Used by US Fed, ECB, Bank of Japan after 2008 financial crisis.

q: India's National Monetization Pipeline (NMP) aims to monetize government/PSU brownfield assets worth approximately:
explain: NMP (August 2021): Rs 6 lakh crore worth of brownfield infrastructure assets to be monetized over 4 years (FY2022-25). Assets: NHAI roads, railway stations, airports, power lines, gas pipelines, telecom towers. NITI Aayog designed it.

id: economics-10-The Repo Rate is the rat
q: The Repo Rate is the rate at which:
opts: Banks borrow from each other overnight
RBI lends short-term funds to commercial banks against government securities
Commercial banks lend to their best customers
explain: Repo Rate: RBI lends money to commercial banks for short periods (usually overnight) against eligible securities. Increasing repo rate makes borrowing costlier → reduces money supply → controls inflation.

q: India's largest agricultural export in recent years has been:
explain: India's top agricultural exports: Non-basmati rice (became no. 1 rice exporter globally), Marine products (mainly vannamei shrimps to USA, Japan, China), Basmati rice, Spices, Sugar, Cotton, Fresh fruits/vegetables. APEDA oversees agricultural exports. India's total agri exports: ~$50 billion (2022-23).

q: The One District One Product (ODOP) initiative under Aatmanirbhar Bharat promotes:
opts: Agricultural products from one district per state
Local products, crafts, and industries that each district is known for
explain: ODOP: each district identifies a signature product (handicraft, GI-tagged item, agricultural produce) for promotion, branding, and export. Started in UP (2018), scaled nationally under Aatmanirbhar Bharat.

q: Primary deficit is defined as:
explain: Primary Deficit = Fiscal Deficit − Interest Payments. It shows deficit excluding past borrowing costs, indicating current policy's fiscal gap.

q: India's 'Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana' (PMGKAY) provides:
opts: Free food grains (5 kg/person/month), over NFSA quota
explain: PMGKAY (2020): free 5 kg food grains per person per month to NFSA beneficiaries (81 crore people) during COVID-19 — in addition to their regular subsidized PDS quota. Extended 8 times. From January 2023: merged with NFSA — food grains under NFSA now FREE (earlier: rice Rs 3, wheat Rs 2). Cost: Rs 2 lakh crore/year approximately.

q: The first Indian bank to be established (1806) was:
opts: Bank of Calcutta (later Bank of Bengal)
explain: Bank of Calcutta (1806) → renamed Bank of Bengal. Three Presidency Banks (Bengal 1806, Bombay 1840, Madras 1843) merged in 1921 to form Imperial Bank of India, which became State Bank of India in 1955.

q: PMAY-G (Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana - Gramin) provides housing assistance of:
opts: Rs 2 lakh for urban areas (that's PMAY-U)
explain: PMAY-G (2016): replaces IAY (Indira Awas Yojana). Financial assistance: Rs 1.20 lakh (plains), Rs 1.30 lakh (hilly/NE). Additionally: Rs 12,000 for toilet under SBM, Rs 18,000 MGNREGA wages for construction, free LPG (PMUY), free electricity connection (Saubhagya). Beneficiary selection: SECC 2011 data. Targets building 2.95 crore houses by 2024.

q:
Consider the following statements on financial inclusion in India:
1. The Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) aims to provide universal access to banking facilities.
2. Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) uses Aadhaar-linked bank accounts to transfer subsidies directly to beneficiaries.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Both are correct — PMJDY targets universal banking access, and DBT relies on Aadhaar-linked accounts (the 'JAM trinity': Jan Dhan, Aadhaar, Mobile) for direct subsidy transfer.

q: The Economic Survey of India is published by:
explain: Economic Survey: prepared by the Economic Division of India's Ministry of Finance (typically under the Chief Economic Adviser to the Government). Released one day before the Union Budget. Provides: macroeconomic overview, sector-wise analysis, fiscal data, and policy recommendations. Since 2017, it has been published in two volumes.

q: The Sovereign Gold Bond (SGB) scheme was launched to:
opts: Reduce physical gold demand via gold-denominated bonds
explain: Sovereign Gold Bonds (2015, RBI issues on behalf of Government): investors buy bonds denominated in gold grams (instead of physical gold). Benefits: 2.5% annual interest on invested amount, gold price appreciation, no storage cost, capital gains exempt on maturity. Reduces gold imports (India imports ~800-900 tons/year).

q: The National Food Security Act (NFSA) 2013 provides subsidized food grains to what percentage of India's population?
explain: NFSA 2013: covers up to 75% rural + 50% urban population = ~67% of total population (~81.35 crore people). Provides 5 kg/person/month at subsidized rates: Rice Rs 3, Wheat Rs 2, Coarse grains Rs 1/kg.

q: The term 'deflation' means:
opts: Sustained fall in the general price level
Decrease in value of currency abroad
Reduction in money supply without price effects
explain: Deflation: persistent fall in general price level. Causes: demand-side collapse, excess supply, tight monetary policy. Dangers: deflationary spiral (debt-deflation: real debt burden rises), reduced investment (prices expected to fall further), falling wages, rising unemployment. Japan's 'lost decade' (1990s-2000s) is example. Central banks try to avoid deflation.

q: GST stands for:
explain: GST (Goods and Services Tax) is a comprehensive indirect tax levied on supply of goods and services across India. It replaced multiple taxes like VAT, service tax, excise duty.

q: The National Pension System (NPS) replaced the Old Pension Scheme (OPS) for Central Government employees from:
explain: NPS (National Pension System, 2004): replaced defined benefit OPS for central government employees joining from January 1, 2004 onwards. Contributory (employee: 10%, employer: 14% for central govt). Market-linked returns. Managed by PFRDA. NPS extended to all citizens in 2009 (Swavalamban/NPS-Lite for unorganized sector).

q: The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) is responsible for:
opts: Operating India's retail payment systems (UPI, RuPay, etc.)
explain: NPCI (2008): non-profit umbrella organization for retail payment systems. Products: RuPay (domestic card network competing with Visa/Mastercard), IMPS (Immediate Payment Service, 24×7), UPI (Unified Payments Interface), NACH (National Automated Clearing House for bulk transactions), BBPS (Bharat Bill Payment System), FASTag (electronic toll collection).

q: The 'poverty trap' is a situation where:
opts: Poor people can't accumulate savings or investment to escape poverty
Poverty is self-fulfilling prophecy due to geography
explain: Poverty Trap (Jeffrey Sachs): poor people/countries stuck in poverty because: too poor to save/invest → capital doesn't accumulate → productivity stays low → income stays low. Solutions: 'Big Push' (massive external aid to break the cycle), conditional cash transfers, microfinance. Counter-view (Daron Acemoglu, James Robinson): institutions matter more than external shocks.

q: The Planning Commission of India was replaced by:
explain: NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) replaced the Planning Commission in January 2015. It serves as a policy think tank.

q: The interest rate on small savings schemes (PPF, NSC, SSY) is set by:
opts: Government of India (Ministry of Finance), revised quarterly
explain: Small Savings Schemes: National Savings Certificate (NSC), Public Provident Fund (PPF), Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana (SSY), Post Office Savings Account, Monthly Income Scheme, Senior Citizens Savings Scheme (SCSS). Rates set by MoF quarterly, benchmarked to G-Sec yields + spread. Shyamala Gopinath Committee (2011) recommended market-linked rates. Popular due to: tax benefits, safety (government guarantee), higher returns vs bank FD.

q: India's 'Twin Balance Sheet' problem (as described in Economic Survey ~2016) refers to:
opts: Stressed bank (NPA) and corporate balance sheets together
Both government and RBI having deficits
Central and state government deficits simultaneously
Current account and fiscal deficits together
explain: Twin Balance Sheet Problem: (1) Banks: accumulated large NPAs (bad loans) from infrastructure sector lending → unable to lend freely. (2) Corporates: over-borrowed during 2007-12 boom → projects stalled, unable to repay. Together: banks couldn't lend (stressed balance sheets), corporates didn't want to borrow (debt-laden). Required: SARFAESI, IBC 2016, recapitalization of banks.

q: India's 'Smart Cities Mission' outcome metric focuses on:
opts: Quality-of-life improvement via smart urban solutions
Only economic growth in selected cities
explain: Smart Cities Mission (June 2015): 100 cities selected via competition ('City Challenge'). Core infrastructure: smart supply of water, assured electricity, sanitation, solid waste management, efficient urban mobility, affordable housing, IT connectivity, e-governance, safety. Area-Based Development (retrofit, redevelop, greenfield) + Pan-City solutions (ICT). Central grant: Rs 500 crore/city (5 years).

q: The concept of 'infant industry protection' argues:
opts: Temporary tariff protection for new industries to grow
explain: Infant Industry Argument (Friedrich List, 1841 — 'National System of Political Economy'): nascent industries with potential scale economies need temporary protection (tariffs, subsidies) against established foreign competitors until they achieve global competitiveness. USA protected its manufacturing (1800s-1900s) with high tariffs. South Korea's POSCO steel. Counter: protection tends to become permanent, breeds inefficiency.

q: Carbon credits are tradable certificates representing:
opts: Permission to emit 1 tonne of CO2 equivalent
explain: Carbon credit: 1 credit = right to emit 1 tonne CO2 equivalent. Companies that reduce emissions below cap earn credits to sell. Cap-and-trade system. Kyoto Protocol established CDM for developing nations.

q:
With reference to Free Trade Agreements (FTAs), consider the following statements:
1. FTAs typically reduce or eliminate tariffs on trade between the signatory countries.
2. India has signed FTAs with several countries and blocs, including ASEAN.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Both are correct — FTAs reduce/eliminate tariffs between signatories, and India has real FTAs including the India-ASEAN FTA.

q: India's Urban Employment Guarantee Scheme (UGEGS) for urban poor was introduced in:
explain: Urban employment guarantee: the PM Garib Kalyan Rojgar Abhiyan (June 2020) provided 125 days of work to returning migrant workers in 116 districts. Rajasthan's Indira Gandhi Shahri Rozgar Guarantee Yojana (2022): 100 days urban employment. Kerala has similar scheme. No national-level urban employment guarantee act yet.

q: Economics is defined as the study of:
opts: Allocating scarce resources to satisfy unlimited wants
explain: Economics (from Greek 'oikonomia' = household management): study of how scarce resources (land, labor, capital, enterprise) are allocated to satisfy unlimited human wants. Alfred Marshall: 'Science of material welfare.' Lionel Robbins: 'Science of choice under scarcity.'

q: CRR (Cash Reserve Ratio) is:
opts: Minimum percentage of deposits banks must keep as cash with RBI — controls money supply
explain: CRR: Commercial banks must maintain a minimum percentage of their Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) as cash with RBI. High CRR reduces money available for lending (tightens money supply). Currently around 4%.

q: The 'Phillips Curve' in economics (A.W. Phillips, 1958) shows:
opts: Inverse relationship between unemployment and inflation
Direct relationship between unemployment and inflation
No relationship between unemployment and inflation
Relationship between GDP and inflation only
explain: Phillips Curve (1958): negative correlation between unemployment and wage inflation in UK data 1861-1957. Policy implication: policymakers can trade-off (accept more inflation for less unemployment). Stagflation of 1970s disproved simple Phillips Curve. Long-run Phillips Curve (Friedman-Phelps): vertical at Natural Rate of Unemployment (NAIRU) — no long-run trade-off.

q: Bharatmala Pariyojana Phase-I focuses on development of:
opts: National highways including ring roads, expressways, economic corridors
explain: Bharatmala Phase-I: 34,800 km of national highways including Economic Corridors, Inter Corridors, Ring Roads, National Corridor Efficiency Improvements. Outlay ~Rs 5.35 lakh crore.

q: PM POSHAN scheme (renamed from Mid-Day Meal in 2021) covers students up to:
explain: PM POSHAN: covers students from pre-primary (Balvatika) to Class VIII in government and government-aided schools. ~11.8 crore students across ~11.2 lakh schools.

q: The Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) was launched to:
explain: SSA (2001): flagship program for universalizing elementary education (RTE Act 2009 gave it constitutional backing). Established/upgraded schools in unserved habitations, recruited teachers, built classrooms. Mid-Day Meal Scheme complemented SSA. In 2018, SSA, RMSA (secondary), and Teacher Education merged into Samagra Shiksha Abhiyan.

q: The term 'trade surplus' means:
explain: Trade Balance = Exports - Imports. Trade Surplus: Exports > Imports (positive balance). Trade Deficit: Imports > Exports (negative balance). India consistently runs a trade deficit (imports more than exports). India's trade deficit ~$240 billion (2022-23). Offset partially by services surplus, remittances. China and Germany have large trade surpluses.

q: India's National Investment and Infrastructure Fund (NIIF) was established to:
opts: Attract long-term domestic and foreign capital for infrastructure
explain: NIIF (2015): quasi-sovereign wealth fund. Master Fund, Fund of Funds, and Strategic Opportunities Fund. Invests in infrastructure (roads, ports, airports, energy). Government owns 49%, rest from global investors.

q: The term 'externality' in economics refers to:
opts: A cost or benefit falling on an uninvolved third party
explain: Externalities: spillover effects on uninvolved parties. Negative: factory pollutes river (costs borne by community, not factory). Positive: education (benefits society beyond individual). Externalities cause market failure (market produces too much pollution, too little education). Government response: taxes (Pigouvian tax on negative), subsidies (positive), regulation.

q: The concept of 'trickle-up economics' (bottom-up growth) argues:
opts: Investing in the poor drives broader economic growth
explain: Bottom-up/inclusive growth: investing in the poor directly (education, health, social protection) → higher productivity, greater consumer demand, reduced inequality → sustainable growth. Evidence from Kerala model, Nordic countries. Contrast with trickle-down (top-first approach). Linked to Amartya Sen's capabilities approach and UNDP's HDI concept.

q: The Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) aims at:
opts: Financial inclusion via zero-balance bank accounts
explain: PMJDY (August 28, 2014): world's largest financial inclusion initiative. Features: zero-balance savings account (Jan Dhan account), RuPay debit card with Rs 2 lakh accident insurance, Rs 30,000 life insurance, Rs 10,000 overdraft facility. By 2024: 52+ crore accounts opened, mostly in rural areas.

q:
Consider the following statements regarding rural indebtedness and land reforms:
1. Land ceiling laws set an upper limit on the amount of agricultural land an individual/family can hold.
2. Tenancy reforms sought to give greater security of tenure to tenant cultivators.
3. The Green Revolution reduced regional disparities in agricultural productivity across all of India uniformly.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
explain: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is incorrect — the Green Revolution's benefits were geographically uneven, concentrated mainly in Punjab, Haryana and western UP, widening rather than reducing regional disparities. Hence 1 and 2 only.

q: The 'Har Ghar Jal' (Jal Jeevan Mission) aims to:
opts: Tap water to every rural household by 2024
explain: Jal Jeevan Mission (Aug 15, 2019): 'Har Ghar Jal' — tap water (Functional Household Tap Connection/FHTC) to every rural household. Target: 55 litres per capita per day (lpcd) potable water. Progress: from 17% coverage (2019) to ~75%+ (2023). Total outlay: Rs 3.60 lakh crore. Implementation: Ministry of Jal Shakti with State governments.

q:
Statement-I: The introduction of GST aimed to create a unified national market in India.
Statement-II: GST replaced a complex web of state-level and central indirect taxes with cascading effects (tax on tax), which had fragmented the domestic market.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
opts: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
explain: Both statements are correct, and the fragmentation/cascading-tax problem described in Statement-II is precisely what GST's unified-market goal in Statement-I was designed to fix.

q: Which ministry is primarily responsible for the development and promotion of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) in India?
explain: The Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) is the dedicated ministry responsible for MSME policy and promotion.

q:
With reference to social security schemes in India, consider the following statements:
1. The Atal Pension Yojana provides a guaranteed minimum pension to subscribers, targeted at unorganised sector workers.
2. Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana provides accident insurance coverage at a low annual premium.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Both are correct — Atal Pension Yojana targets unorganised-sector workers with a guaranteed pension, and PMSBY offers low-premium accident insurance.

q: India's 'JAM Trinity' stands for:
explain: JAM Trinity: proposed by Economic Survey 2014-15 (Arvind Subramanian, Chief Economic Adviser). Jan Dhan: bank accounts for all. Aadhaar: biometric unique ID. Mobile: connectivity and digital payments. JAM enables direct transfer of subsidies (LPG, fertilizer, MGNREGA wages, scholarships) to beneficiaries' accounts — reducing leakage and corruption.

q: The 'Dutch Flower Auction' pricing mechanism is used for:
opts: Price starts high and descends until accepted
Price starting low and going up (English auction)
explain: Dutch (Descending) Auction: auctioneer starts at high price, lowers until a buyer bids. First bidder who accepts becomes the buyer. Advantage: fast (one round). Used in: Dutch flower market (hence name), fish markets, US Treasury auctions (actually uniform price), Google's IPO. Contrasts with English (ascending) auction where price rises until one bidder remains.

q: A 'monopoly' market exists when:
opts: Only one seller, no close substitutes
explain: Monopoly: single seller, many buyers, no close substitutes, high barriers to entry. Monopolist is a price-maker (sets price or quantity, not both simultaneously). Types: natural monopoly (railways, utilities), legal monopoly (patents, copyrights), geographic monopoly. Profits maximized at MR = MC. DPL in distribution, Delhi Metro in metro system are examples.

q: India's first Regional Rural Bank (RRB) was:
explain: Prathama Bank (now Prathama UP Gramin Bank after merger): first RRB established October 2, 1975, Gandhi Jayanti, in Moradabad, UP. Sponsored by Syndicate Bank. 5 RRBs simultaneously established as pilot. Based on Narasimham Committee recommendations (1975). Total 5 initial RRBs: Prathama (Moradabad), Gorakhpur Kshetriya Gramin (UP), Haryana Kshetriya Gramin (Bhiwani), Jaipur Nagaur Anchalik (Rajasthan), Singhbhum (Bihar).

q:
Consider the following statements about India's industrial policy history:
1. The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 classified industries into public, joint and private sectors.
2. The New Industrial Policy of 1991 significantly reduced the scope of industrial licensing.
3. Industrial licensing was abolished for all industries without exception after 1991.
4. The 1991 reforms opened many sectors to foreign direct investment (FDI).
How many of the above statements are correct?
explain: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. Statement 3 is incorrect — licensing was retained for a small list of strategic/sensitive industries (e.g., defence, hazardous chemicals) even after 1991, not abolished universally. Hence only three.

q: Poverty line in India is determined based on:
explain: India's poverty line is primarily based on minimum required calorie intake (2,400 kcal/day rural; 2,100 kcal/day urban) and the expenditure needed to achieve it. The Tendulkar Committee revised this methodology.

q: The MUDRA (Micro Units Development and Refinance Agency) Bank refinances:
opts: MFIs, NBFCs, and banks that lend to small enterprises
explain: MUDRA Bank (2015, subsidiary of SIDBI): does not lend directly to end borrowers. Refinances intermediaries (MFIs, NBFCs, SFBs, RRBs, commercial banks, cooperative banks) that lend to micro and small enterprises. MUDRA also provides credit guarantees. Rs 3 lakh crore disbursed under PM Mudra Yojana since 2015.

q: The term 'Dutch Disease' in economics refers to:
opts: Economic downturn caused by flood/natural disaster
Decline in manufacturing sector caused by a large discovery/boom in natural resources (e.g., oil)
High inflation in a welfare state
Economic recession caused by high wages
explain: Dutch Disease: named after Netherlands' 1960s natural gas discovery. Resource boom → currency appreciates → exports of other sectors (manufacturing) become uncompetitive → deindustrialization. Affects many resource-rich nations.

q: The concept of 'Animal Spirits' in economics, referring to psychological factors driving investment decisions, was introduced by:
explain: Keynes (General Theory, 1936): 'Animal Spirits' = spontaneous optimism or pessimism driving business investment decisions beyond rational calculation. Akerlof & Shiller revived concept in their 2009 book.

q: NABARD's function of refinancing is:
opts: Providing funds to cooperative banks, RRBs, and commercial banks for agri lending
Providing loans directly to farmers only
explain: NABARD refinancing: Short-term credit (seasonal agricultural operations: crop loans) and Long-term credit (land development, farm machinery, irrigation) to: District/State Cooperative Banks, Regional Rural Banks, Commercial Banks. NABARD also gives direct loans to state governments (RIDF — Rural Infrastructure Development Fund) for rural projects.

q: The term 'hollowing out of manufacturing' or 'deindustrialisation' refers to:
opts: Manufacturing's declining share of GDP/employment as economy matures
explain: Premature Deindustrialisation (Dani Rodrik): developing countries' manufacturing peaks at lower income levels than historical norm (as rich countries moved to services). India risk: moving from agriculture directly to services without sufficient manufacturing (at ~14-17% of GDP vs China's peak ~32%). Manufacturing provides scale employment for low-skilled workers — without it, structural transformation is incomplete.

q:
Consider the following statements about NITI Aayog:
1. It replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015.
2. Unlike the Planning Commission, it does not have the power to allocate funds to ministries or states.
3. It functions primarily as a policy think-tank offering strategic and technical advice.
4. It formulates and enforces legally binding Five-Year Plans for all states.
How many of the above statements are correct?
explain: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is incorrect — NITI Aayog does not formulate binding Five-Year Plans; that function ended with the Planning Commission's replacement, and NITI Aayog operates in an advisory, not directive, capacity. Hence only three.

q: The National Housing Bank (NHB) was set up to:
opts: Regulate and refinance housing finance companies
explain: NHB (National Housing Bank, 1988): wholly owned by Government of India since 2019 (RBI transferred its shares). Functions: apex-level institution for housing finance; promotes housing finance institutions; provides refinance to HFCs; regulates/supervises HFCs; raises funds (NHB Bonds). Supervises: HDFC, LIC Housing Finance, PNB Housing, etc.

q: National Commodity and Derivatives Exchange (NCDEX) and MCX are:
explain: Commodity exchanges: MCX (Multi Commodity Exchange, 2003): gold, silver, crude oil, base metals, natural gas. NCDEX (2003): agricultural commodities — chana (chickpea), soybean, guar, turmeric, pepper. FMC (Forward Markets Commission) regulated; merged with SEBI in 2015. Commodity futures allow farmers and traders to hedge price risk.

q: India's services sector contributes approximately what percentage to GDP?
explain: India's GDP composition (2022-23): Services ~55% (IT/ITES, banking, insurance, real estate, trade, transport, tourism, education, health). Industry ~27% (manufacturing, construction, mining). Agriculture ~17% (but employs ~45% of workforce — showing massive productivity gap). India's IT exports (~$250 billion) make it the global IT capital.

q: The Sagarmala Programme focuses on:
opts: Port-led development, coastal shipping, port connectivity
explain: Sagarmala Programme (2015, Ministry of Ports): port modernization, port connectivity, port-led industrialization, and coastal community development. Aims to reduce logistics costs via coastal shipping.

q: India's 'Special Category States' historically included:
explain: Special Category States (SCS): 1969 National Development Council. Criteria: hilly/difficult terrain, low economic base, international borders, sparsely populated. 11 SCS: Arunachal, Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Tripura, Sikkim, HP, Uttarakhand, J&K (now UT). Benefits: 90:10 central funding for CSS (vs 60:40 normal). After 14th FC, special category distinction de-emphasized (higher tax devolution to all).

q:
With reference to MGNREGA (Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act), consider the following statements:
1. It legally guarantees 100 days of wage employment in a financial year to rural households willing to do unskilled manual work.
2. It is a demand-driven scheme, meaning employment must be provided within a stipulated time of being sought.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Both are correct — the 100-day legal guarantee and the demand-driven design are core, accurate features of MGNREGA.

q: Tier 1 capital of a bank consists of:
opts: Core equity capital: paid-up equity, retained earnings, disclosed reserves
Revaluation reserves and investment fluctuation reserves
explain: Tier 1 (Core Capital) = Equity share capital + Retained earnings + Disclosed free reserves. It's the highest quality capital. Tier 2 = Supplementary capital (subordinated debt, revaluation reserves).

q:
With reference to core inflation, consider the following statements:
1. Core inflation excludes volatile components such as food and fuel prices from the CPI basket.
2. It is often considered a better gauge of underlying, persistent inflationary pressure than headline inflation.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Both are correct — core inflation's exclusion of volatile food/fuel components and its use as a signal of persistent inflation are standard macroeconomic concepts.

q: The Agriculture Produce Market Committee (APMC) Act was designed to:
opts: Protect farmers from exploitation by middlemen
explain: APMC Acts (state subject) created regulated mandis to ensure fair prices for farmers. Critics say they create cartels. The three Farm Acts 2020 (later repealed) aimed to allow sales outside APMCs.

q: The term 'balance of payments' refers to:
opts: Record of all economic transactions between a country and the rest of the world
Export value vs import value (Trade Balance)
explain: Balance of Payments (BoP): complete record of all monetary transactions between a country and the rest of the world. Current Account: goods (trade balance), services, income, current transfers. Capital Account: FDI, FPI/FII, loans, banking capital. BoP always balances (accounting identity). BoP crisis: when foreign reserves are insufficient.

q: The National Monetization Pipeline (NMP) was announced by:
explain: NMP (National Monetization Pipeline, 2021-2025): aims to raise Rs 6 lakh crore by transferring operation of existing government assets (brownfield) to private sector for a fixed period (not selling assets). Assets: NHAI roads, railway stations/freight terminals, power lines (PGCIL), gas pipelines (GAIL), airports (AAI), ports. Asset monetization ≠ privatization.

q: e-NAM (electronic National Agriculture Market) is a pan-India online trading platform launched in:
explain: e-NAM launched April 14, 2016 by SFAC (Small Farmers Agribusiness Consortium) under Ministry of Agriculture. Connects APMC mandis online for transparent price discovery.

q: India's Five Year Plans were a feature of which economic model?
explain: India's Five-Year Plans (1951-2017, 12 plans total) were inspired by Soviet Union's central planning model. First Plan (1951-56): agriculture focus (Bhakra dam, community development). Second Plan (Nehru-Mahalanobis): heavy industry. 12th Plan ended 2017. NITI Aayog replaced with strategy documents.

q: The 'Make in India' lion symbol is a:
opts: A walking lion made of cogwheels
explain: Make in India logo: stylized lion (inspired by Ashoka Chakra wheel lion) with body composed of cogwheels/gears — symbolizing manufacturing, industrial growth, and India moving forward. Lion represents strength, boldness. Campaign tagline: 'Make in India' with the lion symbol on all promotions.

q: The Twelfth Finance Commission of India recommended:
opts: Recommends tax devolution between Centre and States (Article 280 body)
explain: Finance Commission (Article 280): constituted every 5 years to recommend: (1) distribution of tax revenue between Centre and States (vertical devolution), (2) distribution among states (horizontal devolution), (3) grants-in-aid to states. 15th FC (N.K. Singh, 2021-26): recommended 41% of divisible pool to states. 14th FC: 42%.

q: India's current account in BoP is in deficit mainly because of:
explain: India's Current Account Deficit (CAD): Main contributor is merchandise trade deficit (imports: crude oil ~20-25% of total imports, gold ~8%, electronic items; exports: engineering goods, petroleum products, chemicals). Partly offset by: services surplus (IT exports ~$250B), remittances (~$100B from NRIs). CAD typically 1-3% of GDP, manageable.

q: India's agricultural marketing is regulated through:
explain: APMC (Agricultural Produce Market Committee) system: most states have APMCs that regulate agricultural markets (mandis). Farmers had to sell produce only through licensed commission agents in regulated markets. Critiqued for middleman exploitation. Model APMC Act 2003: allow private markets, direct farmer-buyer links. Farm Laws 2020 (allowing direct selling, contract farming) were repealed November 2021 after farmer protests.

q: 'Stagflation-proof' growth refers to:
opts: Growth with stable inflation and employment
explain: Ideally, economies want: high economic growth + low inflation + low unemployment. However, this is difficult due to trade-offs (Phillips Curve, inflationary pressures from growth). Supply-side shocks (oil price spikes, pandemics) cause both recession and inflation (stagflation). Structural reforms (improving productivity) can achieve growth with moderate inflation.

q: Which international organisation is primarily responsible for overseeing global trade rules and resolving trade disputes between member nations?
explain: The World Trade Organization (WTO) is the primary international body overseeing global trade rules and dispute resolution.

q: The term 'Helicopter Money' (popularized by Milton Friedman) refers to:
opts: Emergency aid dropped in disaster zones
Central bank directly distributing money to the public to stimulate economy
explain: Helicopter Money: Friedman's metaphor for central bank dropping cash from helicopter (direct transfers to citizens) to stimulate demand. Unlike QE (which goes through banks), helicopter money bypasses banks. Discussed during deflation crises.

q: The 'Human Development Index' (HDI) is published by:
explain: The HDI is published by UNDP in the Human Development Report. It measures countries on three dimensions: life expectancy, education, and per capita income.

q: The National Statistical Office (NSO) is under:
opts: Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI)
explain: NSO (National Statistical Office, formed 2019 by merging CSO — Central Statistics Office and NSSO — National Sample Survey Office): under MoSPI. Compiles: GDP/national accounts, IIP, Consumer Expenditure Survey, Periodic Labour Force Survey, Annual Survey of Industries. Releases: First Advance Estimates (Jan), Revised Estimates, and Final GDP data.

q: The Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) is responsible for:
opts: Formulating and implementing India's Foreign Trade Policy (FTP)
explain: DGFT: under Ministry of Commerce and Industry. Implements FTP, issues Importer Exporter Code (IEC), administers export promotion schemes (EPCG, Advance Authorization, MEIS/RODTEP). Also issues export/import licenses.

q: Microfinance refers to:
opts: Small loans and financial services for low-income people without bank access
explain: Microfinance: pioneered by Muhammad Yunus (Grameen Bank, Bangladesh, 1983 — Nobel Peace Prize 2006). In India: SHG-Bank Linkage Programme (RBI/NABARD, 1992) — women form self-help groups, save collectively, access bank credit. MFIs (Microfinance Institutions) like SKS/Bandhan. India has world's largest microfinance program.

q: The 'Self-Reliant India (Aatmanirbhar Bharat)' initiative was announced in:
explain: Aatmanirbhar Bharat (Self-Reliant India, May 2020): announced during COVID-19 pandemic. Rs 20 lakh crore package (about 10% of GDP: fiscal ~1.7%, liquidity measures ~8.3%). Five pillars: Economy, Infrastructure, System, Demography, Demand. Key elements: PLI schemes, coal auction, defence production, MSME relief, migrant workers' support, agricultural reforms (farm laws — later repealed).

q: India's Foreign Exchange Reserves are managed by:
explain: RBI manages India's foreign exchange reserves: Foreign Currency Assets (FCA, largest component — USD, EUR, GBP, JPY treasury bills and bonds), Gold reserves (~800 tons), Special Drawing Rights (SDRs) from IMF, and Reserve Tranche Position at IMF. Used to: stabilize rupee, manage BoP, instill confidence. India: 4th largest forex reserves globally.

q: SENSEX is the benchmark stock market index of:
explain: SENSEX (Sensitive Index): BSE's 30-stock index. NSE's benchmark: NIFTY 50 (50 stocks). BSE (1875): world's oldest stock exchange in Asia, at Dalal Street, Mumbai. NSE (1992): India's largest exchange by trading volume. SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India, 1992): regulator of securities market.

q:
Consider the following statements about a rise in the general price level, as tested in real PYQs:
1. An increase in money supply, if not matched by output growth, is a possible cause.
2. A decrease in the aggregate level of output for a given money supply is a possible cause.
3. An increase in the effective demand for goods and services in the economy is a possible cause.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
explain: All three are correct — each represents a genuine, textbook mechanism by which the general price level can rise (monetary, supply-side, and demand-side channels). Hence 1, 2 and 3.

q: Human Capital Theory, associated with Gary Becker and Theodore Schultz, argues that:
opts: Physical capital is the only driver of growth
Investment in education and health raises productivity like investment in machines
Trade is the engine of growth
explain: Human Capital Theory: education, health, training are investments that increase individual productivity and economic growth. Schultz won Nobel 1979; Becker won Nobel 1992.

q: WTO replaced which organisation in 1995?
opts: GATT (General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade)
explain: WTO replaced GATT on 1 January 1995 after the Uruguay Round negotiations. WTO administers multilateral trade agreements, provides dispute settlement, and has 164 member countries. HQ: Geneva, Switzerland.

q: The concept of 'moral economy' in the context of peasant societies (James Scott) refers to:
opts: Elites must ensure peasants' subsistence in bad times
explain: Moral Economy (James Scott, 'Moral Economy of the Peasant,' 1976): peasant societies have implicit social contract — in exchange for deference/taxes, elites ensure peasants' survival in bad years (insurance principle). When elites/colonial powers violate this by insisting on market prices (even in famines), peasants rebel. Applied to explain colonial-era famines and peasant revolts in Asia.

q: The 'Monetary Policy Transmission' problem in India means:
opts: RBI rate changes not fully passed on by banks
explain: Monetary Policy Transmission: when RBI cuts repo rate, commercial banks should lower their lending rates (to stimulate growth). Problems in India: banks have legacy fixed-rate deposits (can't reduce cost immediately), MCLR-linked loans take time vs EBLR-linked (quicker). Also: banks may not cut rates if they have high NPAs (risk aversion). EBLR regime (2019): faster transmission for retail loans.

q: India's government spending on education (as % of GDP) target as per NEP 2020 is:
explain: National Education Policy (NEP 2020, first new policy since 1986): recommends public investment in education reaching 6% of GDP (from current ~4.5%). Key reforms: 5+3+3+4 curriculum structure (replacing 10+2), foundational stage focus (up to age 8), vocational education from Class 6, multiple entry/exit in higher education, regional language medium. Implementation challenge: requires doubling of education budget.

q: W.W. Rostow's 'Stages of Economic Growth' identifies how many stages of development?
explain: Rostow (1960): 5 stages — (1) Traditional Society, (2) Pre-conditions for Take-off, (3) Take-off, (4) Drive to Maturity, (5) Age of High Mass Consumption.

q: The term 'current account deficit' (CAD) in India means:
opts: Imports of goods, services, and income exceed exports and transfers
explain: Current Account Deficit (CAD): when the sum of trade deficit + services deficit + net income outflows > net transfers (remittances). India's CAD: typically 1-3% of GDP, mainly due to oil and gold imports. 1991 crisis: CAD became unsustainable. Financed by: FDI, FPI/FII inflows, NRI deposits, ECBs (External Commercial Borrowings).

q: The Green Revolution in India (1960s-70s) was mainly associated with:
opts: HYV seeds, chemical fertilisers, and irrigation for wheat and rice
explain: Green Revolution: Introduction of HYV seeds (Norman Borlaug's wheat, IR8 rice), chemical fertilisers, pesticides, and expanded irrigation transformed Indian agriculture. Led by M.S. Swaminathan in India. Punjab, Haryana, and UP were the main beneficiaries.

q: The Market Stabilization Scheme (MSS) allows RBI to issue government securities to:
opts: Absorb excess liquidity from large capital inflows
explain: MSS (2004): RBI issues T-Bills/dated securities to mop up excess liquidity from large capital inflows. Proceeds held in separate MSS account with RBI (not used for government expenditure). Sterilization tool.

q: The Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) manages:
opts: Provident Fund, Pension Scheme, and Deposit Linked Insurance
explain: EPFO (established 1952, EPF Act 1952): statutory body under Ministry of Labour. Manages: EPF (both contribute 12% of basic+DA; employee's 12% → EPF, employer's 12% → 8.33% EPS + 3.67% EPF), EPS (pension of up to Rs 7,500/month), EDLI (life insurance of up to Rs 7 lakh on death in service). Covers establishments with 20+ employees.

q: Inflation targeting in India means:
opts: RBI mandated to keep CPI inflation at 4% (±2%)
explain: Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT) framework adopted 2016 (RBI Amendment Act): RBI's primary objective is price stability while keeping growth in mind. Target: CPI inflation 4% ±2% (i.e., 2-6%). Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) decides policy rate. If inflation exceeds band for 3 consecutive quarters, RBI must explain reasons and remedial actions to government.

q: The TANGEDCO (Tamil Nadu Generation and Distribution Corporation) was formed by bifurcating which earlier entity?
explain: TNEB was bifurcated in 2010 into TANGEDCO (generation and distribution) and TANTRANSCO (transmission). This complied with the Electricity Act 2003 requirement to unbundle electricity utilities.

q: The National Sample Survey (NSS) / PLFS (Periodic Labour Force Survey) provides data on:
opts: Employment, unemployment, wages, and consumer expenditure
explain: NSO conducts: PLFS (Periodic Labour Force Survey, 2017): quarterly urban data + annual rural+urban data on employment, wages, migration patterns. HCES (Household Consumer Expenditure Survey): spending patterns (last conducted 2022-23 after gap since 2011-12 — 2017-18 data was withheld due to controversy). These surveys inform poverty estimates and policy.

q: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) was established in:
explain: IBBI: established October 1, 2016 under IBC 2016. Regulates insolvency professionals, insolvency professional agencies, information utilities. Its establishment was key to operationalizing IBC.

q: The Delhi-Mumbai Industrial Corridor (DMIC) is a joint initiative with which country?
explain: DMIC: India-Japan joint project along the 1,483-km Western Dedicated Freight Corridor. 24 manufacturing cities/nodes planned across 6 states. Japan invested in DMIC Development Corporation.

q: The 'Big Push' theory of economic development was proposed by:
explain: Big Push Theory (Rosenstein-Rodan, 1943): developing countries face coordination failure — no single entrepreneur invests because market too small, but if all invest simultaneously, market becomes viable. Solution: coordinated, large-scale investment across sectors simultaneously. Influenced India's Five Year Plans (simultaneous industrialization across sectors).

q:
Consider the following statements about the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI):
1. It measures poverty based on indicators across health, education and standard of living.
2. It is a broader concept than income-based poverty measures alone.
3. It was developed jointly with reference to work by the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative (OPHI) and UNDP.
4. India's national MPI framework excludes all health-related indicators.
How many of the above statements are correct?
explain: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is incorrect — India's national MPI (by NITI Aayog) does include health indicators (nutrition, child/adolescent mortality) as one of its three dimensions. Hence only three.

q: The Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR) measures:
opts: Percentage of working-age population that is employed
Percentage of population employed in formal sector
Percentage of working-age population that is employed or actively seeking employment
Percentage of population below poverty line
explain: LFPR = (Labour Force / Working-age Population) × 100. Labour Force = Employed + Unemployed (those seeking jobs). India's female LFPR is among the lowest globally (~25%).

q: The headquarters of RBI is in:
explain: The Reserve Bank of India's headquarters is in Mumbai (Maharashtra). It was originally established in Kolkata in 1935 and moved to Mumbai in 1937.
